before we run new experiments please adapt our setup. we switched to reward bias substitution and need to make our setup work for that. please first make a thorough analysis of which parts of our pipeline need adaption (if any) and then make a plan for this. here our current expose such that you know exactly the current thesis direction: // Master Thesis Exposé, Draft v0.9 (2026-07-31)
// v0.9: review pass. Title softened to "Safer". RLVR-vs-RLHF scope
// caveat added (§3). Protocol extended with an out-of-distribution
// split (§4). Contaminated-success row added to the outcome table
// (§7). Preliminary-results claims tightened to match the run
// records (§8). The dropped reference-policy prescription is now
// recorded as a limitation (§9).
// v0.8: reframed around reward bias substitution (Lamparth et al.
// 2026). Three research questions: effectiveness, side effects, safer
// evaluation. Title block consolidated back to the v0.7 format (one
// title, one subtitle, no separate research-focus block) and the
// citation set restored to the full v0.7 bibliography.
// v0.7: timeline section removed (planning lives in
// thesis/outline.md).
// v0.6: math pilot results removed from the expose; preliminary
// results are agentic-only (OpenEnv is the setting of record).
// Compile with:  typst compile expose.typ   (or ./compile-expose.sh)
//
// Bibliography: refs.yml (Hayagriva format). IEEE style by default.

#set page(
  paper: "a4",
  margin: (x: 2.5cm, y: 2.5cm),
  numbering: "1",
)
#set text(font: "New Computer Modern", size: 11pt, lang: "en")
#set par(justify: true, leading: 0.65em)

#show heading.where(level: 1): set text(size: 13pt)
#show heading.where(level: 2): set text(size: 11.5pt)
#set table(stroke: 0.5pt)

// ---------- Title block ----------
#align(center)[
  #text(size: 16pt, weight: "bold")[
    Safer Reward Shaping for Efficient LLM Agents
  ]

  #text(size: 13pt)[
    Detecting Reward Bias Substitution during On-Demand \
    Specialization with GRPO in OpenEnv
  ]

  #v(0.4cm)
  _Master's Thesis Exposé_ \
  #v(0.2cm)

  #grid(
    columns: (auto, auto),
    column-gutter: 1.5cm,
    row-gutter: 0.3em,
    align: (right, left),
    [*Author:*], [Marcel Heidebrecht],
    [*University:*], [Technische Universität Berlin],
    [*Date:*], [2026-07-31],
  )
]

#v(0.5cm)
#line(length: 100%)

// ---------- 1 Motivation ----------
= Motivation

Reasoning language models often generate more reasoning than a task
requires, a behavior documented across models and benchmarks
@sui2025survey. In an agentic system this cost becomes especially
large, because the model reasons repeatedly across the steps of an
episode. Work on agentic tasks shows that curbing overthinking can cut
compute and raise task success at the same time @cuadron2025agentic,
so reducing unnecessary reasoning could make agents cheaper and, in
some cases, more reliable.

This thesis studies on-demand specialization. When a new recurring
task becomes available, a small language model is fine-tuned with
reinforcement learning to become an expert for that task. The
specialized model should solve the task at least as reliably as the
original model while using less computation. Producing the expert must
itself be cheap, so training cost is a constraint of the method and is
reported alongside what the expert saves at inference.

The main challenge is the reward used during fine-tuning. A simple
reward for shorter reasoning may reduce token usage, but it can also
produce unwanted side effects. For example, an agent may stop too
early, skip necessary reasoning, or claim that a task is complete even
when it is not. The target is not zero tokens either: accuracy does not
keep rising with reasoning length but peaks at a task-dependent
optimum @wu2025length, and pushing thinking past that point can stop
paying off entirely @ghosal2025mirage. Aggregate length is also a
coarse handle, since what makes a trajectory wasteful is which
reasoning segments it spends on rather than how many tokens it
contains @an2025dto.

This problem is related to reward bias substitution
@lamparth2026substitution. Reward bias substitution means that
reducing one unwanted behavior does not necessarily improve the agent
overall. Instead, the agent may shift toward another unwanted
behavior. For example, penalizing long episodes may reduce
non-termination but increase premature termination.

For this reason, it is not sufficient to measure only the behavior
directly targeted by the reward. A reward should be considered
successful only when it reduces computational cost without lowering
task success or creating new undesirable behaviors.

The thesis investigates this problem empirically in a small and
controlled setting using GRPO @shao2024grpo, LoRA, small open language
models, and OpenEnv environments @openenv2025.

// ---------- 2 Research questions ----------
= Research Questions and Objectives

The research questions follow a simple sequence: effectiveness, side
effects, and safer evaluation.

== RQ1 --- Effectiveness of efficiency-oriented reward shaping

*How effectively can reward shaping reduce the reasoning and
interaction cost of a specialized LLM agent while preserving task
success?*

*Objective:* Evaluate whether efficiency-oriented rewards reduce
reasoning tokens, environment interactions, or episode length compared
with task-success-only GRPO, without reducing correct task completion.

== RQ2 --- Reward bias substitution in agentic behavior

*Does reducing one inefficient behavior cause the agent to shift
toward other undesirable behaviors?*

*Objective:* Identify whether improvements in the targeted behavior
are accompanied by off-target changes such as premature disengagement,
insufficient verification, lower task performance, incorrect
completion claims, or other environment-specific behavioral changes.
The agentic overthinking literature supplies the candidate axes
@cuadron2025agentic.

== RQ3 --- Evaluation of safer reward designs

*How can reward formulations be evaluated to distinguish genuine
efficiency improvements from reward bias substitution?*

*Objective:* Develop and apply a practical evaluation protocol that
jointly considers the targeted efficiency change, overall task
performance, and relevant off-target changes on trajectories generated
by the trained policy. The protocol earns its cost only if it changes
a verdict, so the concrete success criterion is that it identifies at
least one reward setting that a conventional evaluation of targeted
efficiency plus task success would have accepted. If no setting
produces such a case, the thesis reports that no substitution was
found within the measured panel, which is a weaker but still
informative outcome.

// ---------- 3 Reward bias substitution ----------
= Reward Bias Substitution in the Agentic Setting

Lamparth et al. define reward bias substitution as a failure mode in
which suppressing one reward-relevant feature redirects optimization
pressure toward another correlated feature rather than removing the
underlying bias @lamparth2026substitution. Their GRPO example targets
response length and observes a shift toward overconfidence together
with lower free-form factual accuracy. The effect requires only that
the candidate features are mutually correlated and each partially
informative about quality, which is the ordinary case rather than an
edge case.

In OpenEnv, the relevant object is not only a final response but a
complete trajectory containing observations, reasoning, actions, tool
calls, and stopping decisions. Reward bias substitution is therefore
defined operationally as follows:

#block(inset: (left: 1cm, right: 1cm))[
  *A shaped reward reduces its targeted inefficiency, but the trained
  agent shows a systematic deterioration in another relevant behavior
  or in independently measured task quality.*
]

Examples include a reduction in non-termination accompanied by more
premature stopping, or shorter reasoning accompanied by fewer
verification steps and worse performance on difficult tasks. A
mechanism for the second case is already documented: a small minority
of high-entropy tokens carries the branching decisions of a reasoning
trace @wang2025entropy, so pressure against length can remove exactly
the exploration that hard instances need. The thesis will not attempt
to enumerate every possible failure in advance. Instead, it will select
a small set of plausible off-target outcomes for the chosen
environment and interpret them together with task success.

One difference between the two settings has to be stated explicitly,
because it determines how much of the paper transfers. The paper
studies a learned proxy reward model, where the optimized reward and
the true objective diverge by construction and the correlated features
are artifacts of preference learning. This thesis uses a verifiable
environment reward, so on the training task distribution the optimized
reward and the measured objective coincide, and the channel that
carries the paper's headline result, a reward model that treats
expressed confidence as a proxy for quality, is absent. What does
transfer is the shaping term itself: a penalty subtracted from the task
reward is a single-axis operator regardless of what it is added to, and
the pressure it frees can still move any correlated behavior the agent
is able to express. The paper's magnitudes therefore do not carry over,
and whether comparable substitution occurs under a verifiable reward at
all is an open question that this thesis is positioned to answer.

// ---------- 4 Evaluation protocol ----------
= Evaluation Protocol for Safer Reward Design <sec:protocol>

The protocol adapts the paper's central recommendation to agentic RL:
reward shaping must be evaluated after optimization, on trajectories
generated by the resulting policy. Audit metrics computed on
pre-collected data are not sufficient, because the policy itself
changes the distribution of behavior @lamparth2026substitution.

+ *Train a separate policy for each reward condition.* Each reward
  formulation produces a new GRPO policy rather than being evaluated
  only on previously collected trajectories.
+ *Evaluate on fresh held-out tasks, on and off the training
  distribution.* Each trained policy generates new OpenEnv trajectories
  on a held-out split of the training task distribution and on a
  shifted split. The second split carries most of the diagnostic
  weight: because a verifiable reward coincides with the measured
  objective on the training distribution, any true cost of the shaping
  term is most likely to surface off it.
+ *Measure three general dimensions.* Report task performance, the
  targeted efficiency behavior, and a small set of plausible off-target
  behaviors relevant to the environment.
+ *Vary reward strength.* Use several values of the penalty coefficient
  to distinguish insufficient pressure, useful shaping, and
  overcorrection.
+ *Interpret outcomes jointly.* A decrease in tokens or episode length
  is considered successful only when task quality is preserved and no
  relevant off-target deterioration is observed.

// ---------- 5 Metrics transfer ----------
= From the Paper's Metrics to OpenEnv <sec:metrics>

The paper tracks response length, correctness, confidence calibration,
and sycophancy @lamparth2026substitution. These exact metrics are
useful for conversational question answering, but they do not all
transfer directly to every OpenEnv task. The correct transfer is
functional: preserve the roles of the metrics while adapting them to
sequential agent behavior, for which the agentic overthinking
literature provides the behavioral vocabulary @cuadron2025agentic.

#table(
  columns: (auto, auto, 1fr),
  table.header(
    [*Role in the paper*], [*Paper example*], [*OpenEnv counterpart*],
  ),
  [Targeted feature],
  [Response length],
  [Reasoning tokens, interaction steps, or non-termination],

  [Independent task quality],
  [MMLU and TriviaQA accuracy],
  [Verified task completion on held-out environment instances],

  [Off-target behavior],
  [Confidence calibration],
  [Premature stopping, reduced verification, or unsupported
   completion],

  [Additional off-target behavior],
  [Sycophancy / answer flipping],
  [Action instability, unnecessary switching, or sensitivity to
   misleading observations],

  [Optimization diagnostics],
  [Reward scale and policy change],
  [Reward components, KL divergence, and training stability],
)

For the master's thesis, the mandatory evaluation can remain compact:

- Task success: whether the final environment goal is correctly
  achieved.
- Efficiency: reasoning tokens, interaction steps, or episode length.
- Completion behavior: whether the agent terminates successfully, does
  not terminate, or stops prematurely.
- One or two environment-specific off-target indicators, chosen after
  the main OpenEnv task is fixed.

Confidence calibration can be reused directly if the agent can report a
meaningful confidence estimate. Sycophancy should only be reused when
the environment contains user correction or misleading feedback.
Otherwise, agent-specific trajectory measures are more appropriate.

// ---------- 6 Experimental setup ----------
= Experimental Setup and Plan

The base model is a small open LLM, initially Qwen3-1.7B, adapted with
LoRA and trained using GRPO @shao2024grpo. Training and evaluation use
OpenEnv @openenv2025, the open environment-interface library started by
Meta's PyTorch team and Hugging Face, in which an environment is a
server with a Gym-style reset/step contract that executes tool calls
and scores the episode. Classic agentic benchmarks such as ALFWorld
@shridhar2021alfworld and WebShop @yao2022webshop each ship their own
harness, whereas OpenEnv puts a growing catalog of environments behind
one interface. That property is what the on-demand story needs: a new
task class is a new environment behind an unchanged interface, so
specializing for it means pointing the same training loop at a
different environment server. The task-success-only GRPO policy is the
main baseline, because efficiency rewards must improve on an already
specialized agent, not only on the raw model.

== Reward conditions

*E0 --- Base model:* No environment-specific RL post-training.

*E1 --- Task-success baseline:* GRPO with the environment task reward
only.

*E2 --- Length-aware reward:* Task reward minus a penalty for
reasoning or total generated tokens. Because accuracy peaks at an
interior, difficulty-dependent length @wu2025length, the
correctness-coupled variant of this penalty follows DIET
@chen2025diet, which aims the model at that optimum instead of at zero
tokens.

*E3 --- Non-termination-aware reward:* Task reward minus a penalty for
episodes that do not terminate successfully.

*Optional E4 --- Combined reward:* A combination of the strongest
individual conditions, only if time and compute permit.

A general shaped reward is:

#align(center)[
  $R_lambda = R_"task" - lambda dot C_"target"$
]

== Lambda variation

A small sweep is sufficient for the thesis. The exact numerical scale
depends on the reward magnitudes, but the experiment should include:

- $lambda = 0$: task-success-only baseline
- $lambda_"low"$: weak efficiency pressure
- $lambda_"medium"$: moderate efficiency pressure
- $lambda_"high"$: strong efficiency pressure

The coefficients should be selected so that the efficiency component
spans a meaningful range relative to the task reward. A short pilot can
determine concrete values. The key analysis plots task success,
targeted efficiency, and off-target behavior as functions of $lambda$.

== Experimental phases

*Phase 1:* Consolidate the existing controlled pilot and the
success-only baseline.

*Phase 2:* Establish the task-success-only policy in one sequential
OpenEnv environment. The environment is not yet fixed. A
document-grounded question-answering environment and a Python
execution environment are already integrated and are the current
candidates. Two considerations govern the choice. The environment
reward must be goal-grounded rather than satisfied by any successful
tool call, since a task-blind reward cannot carry a training signal;
an environment was already rejected on exactly this ground. And the
observed failure mode of the pilot is non-termination, so the wider
off-target panel in @sec:metrics requires an environment in which
behaviors such as reduced verification or action instability can occur
at all.

*Phase 3:* Run the length-aware and non-termination-aware lambda
sweeps.

*Phase 4:* Repeat the baseline and the most informative reward
settings across at least two seeds.

*Optional Phase 5:* Test the strongest setting on a harder task split
or a second environment.

// ---------- 7 Interpretation ----------
= Interpretation of Outcomes

#table(
  columns: (auto, 1fr),
  table.header([*Outcome*], [*Interpretation*]),

  [Successful reward shaping],
  [The targeted inefficiency decreases, task success is preserved, and
   no relevant off-target deterioration is observed.],

  [Contaminated success],
  [The targeted inefficiency decreases and task success is preserved or
   improves, but an off-target behavior shifts alongside it. The gain
   can mask the shift, which makes this the outcome most easily
   misreported as a clean result.],

  [No meaningful effect],
  [The targeted behavior does not change substantially.],

  [Overcorrection],
  [The targeted inefficiency decreases, but task success deteriorates
   without a clear substitute behavior.],

  [Possible reward bias substitution],
  [The targeted inefficiency decreases, but another undesirable
   behavior increases or independent task quality declines alongside an
   off-target shift.],
)

Because the off-target panel is necessarily incomplete, the thesis
should state that no substitution was detected within the measured
indicators rather than claiming that a reward is universally safe
@lamparth2026substitution.

A campaign in which every reward condition lands in the no-effect row
remains a reportable result rather than a failed thesis. It locates the
point at which a shaped reward stops having any optimization footprint,
which is itself a constraint on where efficiency rewards are worth
applying, and the preliminary results below already contain one such
case.

// ---------- 8 Preliminary results ----------
= Preliminary Results

The current pipeline has completed an initial campaign using Qwen3-1.7B
in an OpenEnv polynomial-equation setting. Task-success-only GRPO
reaches a task success of 0.84, replicated across two training seeds,
against a base-model probe of 0.64. Each expert costs approximately six
hours on one L4 GPU. This is the cost receipt that on-demand
specialization requires. The size of the lift is not yet precise: the
base-model probe used a smaller evaluation sample and its confidence
interval touches that of the trained policy, so a larger base-model
evaluation is queued before the number is reported as final.

The tested cosine length reward @chen2025diet does not produce
additional compression and does not substantially change task success,
at any weight from 1 to 16 and under either composition rule. The logs
suggest that correct episodes are already close to their required
reasoning length, while much of the wasted computation occurs in
incorrect, non-terminating episodes. The targeted axis did not move,
which points to no meaningful effect rather than reward bias
substitution. That reading is not yet conclusive. The shaping component
contributed between fourteen and twenty-seven times more to the
composed advantage than the environment reward, so optimization
pressure was applied and produced no visible change, and no off-target
indicators were logged in that campaign. Separating a genuine
non-effect from an unobserved shift is precisely what the panel in
@sec:protocol is for.

The next central experiment applies a non-termination penalty. The
evaluation will test not only whether non-termination decreases, but
also whether the agent instead stops prematurely, claims completion
incorrectly, or produces shorter unsuccessful trajectories.

// ---------- 9 Contribution and scope ----------
= Expected Contribution and Scope

The thesis contributes an empirical transfer of reward bias
substitution from single-response reward shaping
@lamparth2026substitution to sequential LLM-agent trajectories. It
provides a controlled comparison of efficiency rewards and a practical
protocol for evaluating whether apparent efficiency improvements are
genuine or accompanied by off-target behavioral changes.

The scope is intentionally limited to one small model, one main
sequential OpenEnv environment, the existing controlled pilot, two
reward interventions, and a small lambda sweep. One of the paper's
recommendations is not adopted in full: validating a mitigation against
at least two reference policies of different lineages
@lamparth2026substitution. At roughly six hours per expert on a single
GPU, that is affordable only as a one-off check on the strongest
configuration, and every other result is reported for a single
reference policy. The thesis does not aim to provide a universal
detector of all possible off-target behavior or a formal safety
guarantee.

// ---------- Bibliography ----------
#bibliography("refs.yml", style: "ieee", title: [References])

# Karpathy Guidelines

Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes, derived from [Andrej Karpathy's observations](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876) on LLM coding pitfalls.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:
- State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
- If multiple interpretations exist, present them - don't pick silently.
- If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
- If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

- No features beyond what was asked.
- No abstractions for single-use code.
- No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
- No error handling for impossible scenarios.
- If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:
- Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
- Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
- Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
- If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:
- Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.
- Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:
- "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
- "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
- "Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
```
1. [Step] → verify: [check]
2. [Step] → verify: [check]
3. [Step] → verify: [check]
```

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

# i-have-adhd

The reader has ADHD. Output is not just brief. It is shaped so an ADHD brain can act on it.

## What ADHD changes about reading

Five facts drive every rule below:

1. Working memory is small. Anything not on screen is forgotten. Do not ask the reader to "keep in mind X."
2. Knowing the answer is not doing the answer. The friction between "got it" and "done it" is where work dies.
3. Starting is the hardest step. The first action must be obvious, small, and doable now.
4. Time estimates feel uniform. "A bit of work" and "a few hours" register the same. Vague estimates fail.
5. Dopamine is scarce. Visible progress matters. Buried wins do not register.

## Rules

### 1. Lead with the next action

The first line is something the reader can do. Not context. Not a plan. The action.

Bad: "Let's think about this. Your auth flow has a few moving pieces..."
Good: "Run `npm install jsonwebtoken`, then edit `src/auth.ts:42`."

If the answer is a command, path, or snippet, it goes first. Prose comes after, if at all.

### 2. Number multi-step tasks

If the work takes more than one step, write a numbered list. Each step is one bounded action. No step contains "and then" twice.

Bad: "First open the file, find the function, swap it out, then run the tests."

Good:
```
1. Open `src/auth.ts`
2. Replace `verifyToken` (lines 42 to 58) with the snippet below
3. Run `npm test -- auth.spec.ts`
```

### 3. End with one concrete next action

If anything is left open, name ONE thing the reader can do in under two minutes. Even "open the file" counts.

Bad: "Hope that helps. Let me know if you want to dig deeper."
Good: "Next: run `npm test` and paste the first failing line."

### 4. Suppress tangents

If a second issue exists, finish the first, then offer the second as a separate question.

Bad: "Here's the fix. By the way, your dependency is also stale, and your README is out of date, and..."
Good: "Here's the fix. Separately: there is also a stale dependency. Want me to handle that next?"

### 5. Restate state every turn

The reader cannot hold "we are on step 3 of 5" between messages. Restate it.

Bad: "Done. Ready for the next part?"
Good: "Step 3 of 5 done: schema updated. Next: backfill the new column. Run the script?"

### 6. Give specific time estimates

Vague estimates fail. Ballpark in concrete units.

Bad: "This will take some work."
Good: "About 15 minutes if tests already cover this. An afternoon if not."

### 7. Make completed work visible

Show what now works, in concrete terms. Do not bury wins in a recap.

Bad: "I've made some changes to the auth flow. Among other things..."
Good: "Login now works with magic links. Try: `npm run dev`, open `/login`."

### 8. Matter-of-fact tone for errors

Never use "Uh oh," "Oh no," or "There seems to be a problem." State cause and fix.

Bad: "Uh oh, the test is failing. There seems to be an issue..."
Good: "Test fails at `auth.spec.ts:42`: expected 200, got 401. Cause: missing auth header. Fix: add `Authorization: Bearer ${token}` to the request."

### 9. Cap lists at 5 items

If a list grows past five, split into "do now" vs "later," or "must" vs "nice to have." Five items ranked beats ten unranked.

### 10. No preamble, no recap, no closing pleasantries

Forbidden openers: "Great question," "Let me...", "I'll...", "Sure!", "Looking at your...", "To answer your question..."

Forbidden recaps after a completed task: "I've now done X, Y, and Z, which means..."

Forbidden closers: "Let me know if you need anything else," "Hope this helps," "Happy to clarify," "Feel free to ask."

Start with the answer. End when the answer is done.

## When to break the rules

Override the defaults when:

1. User asks to "explain" or "walk me through." Explain fully. Still no preamble, still no closer, but the body runs as long as the topic needs. Add headers so the reader can skim back.
2. Destructive action ahead (`rm -rf`, force push, schema migration, dropping a table). Confirm before acting. Safety wins over brevity.
3. Debug spiral. If the last three turns have been "still broken," stop iterating on code. Name the assumption that might be wrong. Ask one diagnostic question.
4. Real ambiguity in the request. One short clarifying question beats guessing and rewriting.

## Pre-send check

Before sending, delete:

1. The first sentence if it announces what you are about to do.
2. The last sentence if it asks "anything else?" or recaps what just happened.
3. Any "by the way" sidebar.
4. Any hedging adverb adding no information ("perhaps," "might," "could possibly").

Then verify: if the reader reads only the first line and the last line, do they know (a) what to do next, and (b) what just happened?

If yes, send.

59	def _bootstrap_ci(values: np.ndarray, n_bootstrap: int = N_BOOTSTRAP, ci: float = 0.95) -> tuple[float, float]:
60	    """Bootstrap CI for the mean of continuous `values` (e.g. token counts).
61	    Vectorized: one (n_bootstrap, n) index draw instead of a Python loop, so
62	    10k replicates cost about what 2k used to. Deterministic via fixed RNG seed.
63	
64	    For a binary proportion (accuracy, thinking rates) prefer `_wilson_ci`:
65	    a percentile bootstrap on a 0/1 vector collapses to a zero-width [p, p]
66	    interval at p=0 or p=1, hiding all uncertainty.
67	    """
68	    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
69	    n = len(values)
70	    if n == 0:
71	        return 0.0, 0.0
72	    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
73	    idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=(n_bootstrap, n))
74	    boot = values[idx].mean(axis=1)
75	    alpha = (1 - ci) / 2
76	    return float(np.percentile(boot, 100 * alpha)), float(np.percentile(boot, 100 * (1 - alpha)))
77	
78	
79	def _wilson_ci(n_success: int, n: int, ci: float = 0.95) -> tuple[float, float]:
80	    """Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion. Unlike a
81	    percentile-bootstrap on the 0/1 vector, it stays a proper interval at the
82	    boundaries: 6/6 -> ~[0.61, 1.0] rather than the degenerate [1.0, 1.0].
83	    Clamped to [0, 1]; returns (0, 0) for n=0.
84	    """
85	    if n == 0:
86	        return 0.0, 0.0
87	    z = float(norm.ppf(1 - (1 - ci) / 2))
88	    phat = n_success / n
89	    denom = 1 + z * z / n
90	    center = (phat + z * z / (2 * n)) / denom
91	    half = (z / denom) * np.sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n))
92	    return max(0.0, center - half), min(1.0, center + half)

95	def _thinking_rate(
96	    all_tokens: np.ndarray,
97	    corrects: np.ndarray,
98	    percentile: int,
99	    override: float | None,
100	    side: str,
101	    n_bootstrap: int = N_BOOTSTRAP,
102	    ci: float = 0.95,
103	) -> tuple[float | None, float | None, float | None, float | None]:
104	    """Over/under-thinking rate with a CI that reflects threshold uncertainty.
105	
106	    `side` is 'under' (token <= threshold) or 'over' (token > threshold). The
107	    rate is the fraction of CORRECT completions on the matching side. The
108	    threshold is the `percentile` of ALL token counts (correct + incorrect),
109	    unless `override` is set.
110	
111	    Returns (rate, threshold, ci_low, ci_high), or all-None when there are no
112	    correct samples.
113	
114	    Two CI regimes:
115	      - override set -> threshold is fixed, so the rate is a clean proportion;
116	        use Wilson (no boundary collapse at rate 0/1).
117	      - percentile -> the threshold is itself estimated, so recompute it inside
118	        every bootstrap replicate; its variance then enters the CI (T2.3).
119	    """
120	    all_tokens = np.asarray(all_tokens, dtype=float)
121	    corrects = np.asarray(corrects, dtype=bool)
122	    n = len(all_tokens)
123	    n_correct = int(corrects.sum())
124	    if n_correct == 0:
125	        return None, None, None, None
126	
127	    thr = float(override) if override is not None else float(np.percentile(all_tokens, percentile))
128	    flagged = (all_tokens <= thr) if side == "under" else (all_tokens > thr)
129	    rate = float(flagged[corrects].mean())
130	
131	    if override is not None:
132	        k = int(flagged[corrects].sum())
133	        lo, hi = _wilson_ci(k, n_correct, ci)
134	        return rate, thr, lo, hi
135	
136	    # Percentile threshold: resample all samples, recompute the threshold per
137	    # replicate, then the rate over the resampled correct subset.
138	    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
139	    idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=(n_bootstrap, n))
140	    bt = all_tokens[idx]                                   # (B, n)
141	    bc = corrects[idx]                                     # (B, n)
142	    thr_b = np.percentile(bt, percentile, axis=1, keepdims=True)  # (B, 1)
143	    flag_b = (bt <= thr_b) if side == "under" else (bt > thr_b)
144	    num = (flag_b & bc).sum(axis=1)
145	    den = bc.sum(axis=1)
146	    valid = den > 0
147	    if not valid.any():
148	        return rate, thr, rate, rate
149	    rates = num[valid] / den[valid]
150	    alpha = (1 - ci) / 2
151	    return rate, thr, float(np.percentile(rates, 100 * alpha)), float(np.percentile(rates, 100 * (1 - alpha)))

154	def compute_metrics(
155	    results: list[SampleResult],
156	    underthinking_percentile: int = 10,
157	    overthinking_percentile: int = 75,
158	    n_bootstrap: int = N_BOOTSTRAP,
159	    underthinking_threshold: float | None = None,
160	    overthinking_threshold: float | None = None,
161	) -> EvalMetrics:
162	    """
163	    Compute all thesis metrics from per-sample results.
164	
165	    underthinking_rate: fraction of CORRECT completions whose token count is
166	    at or below the per-split percentile (default P10) of ALL completions.
167	    Flags correct answers produced with unusually little reasoning relative
168	    to the split — likely lucky pattern-matching rather than genuine
169	    derivation. The threshold adapts to dataset verbosity so the metric
170	    behaves consistently across GSM-8K (short) and MATH (long).
171	
172	    overthinking_rate: fraction of CORRECT completions whose token count exceeds
173	    the per-split percentile (default P75) of ALL completions' token counts.
174	    Captures wasted reasoning — the inverse failure mode to underthinking.
175	    Both thresholds are computed over all samples (correct + incorrect) so the
176	    threshold reflects the population's overall verbosity, not just the
177	    correct-subset distribution. Requires at least 4 samples for the
178	    percentile to be meaningful.
179	
180	    pearson_difficulty_length: Pearson r between difficulty score and mean token count.
181	    Positive r means the model spends more tokens on harder problems - desired behaviour.
182	    Requires difficulty labels (MATH levels 1-5); returns None for GSM-8K / DAPO.
183	
184	    accuracy_ci_low/high: 95% bootstrap confidence interval for accuracy.
185	    """
186	    if not results:
187	        return EvalMetrics()
188	
189	    n = len(results)
190	    n_correct = sum(r.correct for r in results)
191	    accuracy = n_correct / n
192	
193	    all_tokens = np.array([r.n_tokens for r in results], dtype=float)
194	    mean_tokens = float(all_tokens.mean())
195	    tokens_ci_low, tokens_ci_high = _bootstrap_ci(all_tokens, n_bootstrap=n_bootstrap)
196	
197	    steps = [r.n_steps for r in results if r.n_steps is not None]
198	    mean_steps = float(np.mean(steps)) if steps else None
199	
200	    correct_results = [r for r in results if r.correct]
201	
202	    # Absolute-threshold overrides (e.g. from a fixed reference run via
203	    # load_reference_thresholds) take precedence over the per-run percentile.
204	    # When set, they make the over/under-thinking rate comparable across runs;
205	    # when None we fall back to the per-run percentile (back-compatible). An
206	    # override also bypasses the n>=4 percentile-stability guard, since the
207	    # threshold no longer depends on this run's sample size.
208	    under_override = underthinking_threshold
209	    over_override = overthinking_threshold
210	
211	    # Both under- and overthinking use a per-split percentile of all token
212	    # counts as the threshold (unless overridden), then count correct samples
213	    # on the matching side. Thresholds are computed once on the observed sample
214	    # and held fixed during the bootstrap — the reported CI is on the rate
215	    # conditional on the observed threshold.
216	    corrects_mask = np.array([r.correct for r in results], dtype=bool)
217	
218	    # Over/under-thinking rates. The threshold (per-split percentile of all token
219	    # counts, or a fixed reference override) is itself estimated, so T2.3
220	    # recomputes it inside each bootstrap replicate to fold its variance into the
221	    # CI — unless an absolute override fixes it, where a Wilson interval on the
222	    # clean proportion is exact. The n>=4 guard keeps the percentile stable; an
223	    # override bypasses it (the threshold no longer depends on this sample size).
224	    underthinking_rate = underthinking_threshold = None
225	    under_ci_low = under_ci_high = None
226	    if correct_results and (n >= 4 or under_override is not None):
227	        underthinking_rate, underthinking_threshold, under_ci_low, under_ci_high = _thinking_rate(
228	            all_tokens, corrects_mask, underthinking_percentile, under_override, "under",
229	            n_bootstrap=n_bootstrap,
230	        )
231	
232	    overthinking_rate = overthinking_threshold = None
233	    over_ci_low = over_ci_high = None
234	    if correct_results and (n >= 4 or over_override is not None):
235	        overthinking_rate, overthinking_threshold, over_ci_low, over_ci_high = _thinking_rate(
236	            all_tokens, corrects_mask, overthinking_percentile, over_override, "over",
237	            n_bootstrap=n_bootstrap,
238	        )
239	
240	    # Accuracy CI: Wilson, not a percentile bootstrap on the binary vector (which
241	    # collapses to [1, 1] at acc=1.0 — the capability_floor 6/6 case).
242	    ci_low, ci_high = _wilson_ci(n_correct, n)
243	
244	    pearson_val = None
245	    pearson_p = None
246	    with_difficulty = [(r.difficulty, r.n_tokens) for r in results if r.difficulty is not None]
247	    if len(with_difficulty) >= 10:
248	        difficulties = [d for d, _ in with_difficulty]
249	        lengths = [l for _, l in with_difficulty]
250	        # pearsonr returns NaN with a warning when either input is constant.
251	        # Skip the call entirely so the report stays free of NaNs.
252	        if len(set(difficulties)) > 1 and len(set(lengths)) > 1:
253	            r_val, p_val = pearsonr(difficulties, lengths)
254	            pearson_val = float(r_val)
255	            pearson_p = float(p_val)
256	
257	    return EvalMetrics(
258	        accuracy=accuracy,
259	        accuracy_ci_low=ci_low,
260	        accuracy_ci_high=ci_high,
261	        mean_token_count=mean_tokens,
262	        mean_token_count_ci_low=tokens_ci_low,
263	        mean_token_count_ci_high=tokens_ci_high,
264	        underthinking_rate=underthinking_rate,
265	        underthinking_rate_ci_low=under_ci_low,
266	        underthinking_rate_ci_high=under_ci_high,
267	        underthinking_threshold=underthinking_threshold,
268	        overthinking_rate=overthinking_rate,
269	        overthinking_rate_ci_low=over_ci_low,
270	        overthinking_rate_ci_high=over_ci_high,
271	        overthinking_threshold=overthinking_threshold,
272	        pearson_difficulty_length=pearson_val,
273	        pearson_p_value=pearson_p,
274	        mean_steps=mean_steps,
275	        n_samples=n,
276	        n_correct=n_correct,
277	        raw=results,
278	    )

281	def load_reference_thresholds(
282	    report_path: str,
283	    under_pct: int = 10,
284	    over_pct: int = 75,
285	    min_samples: int = 4,
286	) -> dict[str, dict]:
287	    """Derive fixed over/under-thinking thresholds from a reference eval report.
288	
289	    Reads `report_path` (a run's eval_report.json) and, for each split that
290	    carries a `samples` series, returns the P`under_pct`/P`over_pct` of its token
291	    counts. Thresholds are kept PER SPLIT on purpose: GSM-8K (id_split) and MATH
292	    (near_ood) have legitimately different verbosity, so a single global
293	    threshold would mislabel one of them. Feed the e0 accuracy-only baseline here
294	    so every run's thinking rates are measured against the same yardstick.
295	
296	    Returns `{split: {"underthinking_threshold": float, "overthinking_threshold": float}}`,
297	    skipping splits with fewer than `min_samples` samples.
298	    """
299	    with open(report_path) as f:
300	        report = json.load(f)
301	    out: dict[str, dict] = {}
302	    for split, metrics in (report.get("results") or {}).items():
303	        samples = (metrics or {}).get("samples")
304	        if not samples or len(samples) < min_samples:
305	            continue
306	        tokens = np.array([s["n_tokens"] for s in samples], dtype=float)
307	        out[split] = {
308	            "underthinking_threshold": float(np.percentile(tokens, under_pct)),
309	            "overthinking_threshold": float(np.percentile(tokens, over_pct)),
310	        }
311	    return out

34	def _build_token_entropy(domain, runner, training_cfg, cfg):
35	    # `fork_mask_top_pct` is deprecated; prefer `fork_mask_top_frac`. Keep
36	    # the old key working for now so existing configs don't break, but
37	    # emit a one-line warning so they get migrated.
38	    if "fork_mask_top_pct" in cfg and "fork_mask_top_frac" not in cfg:
39	        print(
40	            "Warning: rewards.token_entropy.fork_mask_top_pct is deprecated; "
41	            "rename to fork_mask_top_frac (value range [0, 1])."
42	        )
43	    frac = cfg.get("fork_mask_top_frac", cfg.get("fork_mask_top_pct", 0.0))
44	    # Honour explicit max_seq_length on the model config so the entropy
45	    # forward pass doesn't silently exceed the configured context.
46	    model_cfg = getattr(runner, "config", {}).get("model", {}) if hasattr(runner, "config") else {}
47	    max_seq = model_cfg.get("max_seq_length") or training_cfg.get("max_seq_length")
48	    # chunk_size default: vLLM co-resident -> 1 (tight VRAM, see token_entropy
49	    # OOM); otherwise 4 (ample headroom on 24 GB). Override per-config via
50	    # `rewards.token_entropy.chunk_size`.
51	    default_chunk = 1 if model_cfg.get("use_vllm") else 4
52	    chunk_size = int(cfg.get("chunk_size", default_chunk))
53	    return TokenEntropyReward(
54	        runner.model,
55	        runner.tokenizer,
56	        reward_scale=cfg.get("reward_scale", 0.1),
57	        fork_mask_top_frac=frac,
58	        max_seq_length=int(max_seq) if max_seq is not None else None,
59	        chunk_size=chunk_size,
60	    )

4	# module can be imported (and the torch-free NaiveSumComposer / metric draining

8	def _group_indices(prompts) -> list[list[int]]:
9	    """Partition completions into prompt-groups for per-group z-scoring.
10	
11	    TRL GRPOTrainer's reward function receives `prompts` of length
12	    batch_size * num_generations, with each prompt repeated num_generations
13	    times *consecutively*. We rely on that ordering and compare each prompt
14	    to its predecessor with `==` only — no hashing, so no chance of a
15	    64-bit collision merging two distinct prompts into one group.
16	
17	    Returns a list of index-lists, one per group.
18	    """
19	    if not prompts:
20	        return []
21	    groups: list[list[int]] = []
22	    cur: list[int] = [0]
23	    for i in range(1, len(prompts)):
24	        if prompts[i] == prompts[i - 1]:
25	            cur.append(i)
26	        else:
27	            groups.append(cur)
28	            cur = [i]
29	    groups.append(cur)
30	    return groups

33	def _drain_step_metrics(composer) -> dict:
34	    """Average a composer's buffered per-step component metrics across this
35	    step's reward-fn calls, then clear the buffer. Shared by both composers.
36	    """
37	    buf = composer._step_metrics
38	    if not buf:
39	        return {}
40	    agg: dict[str, float] = {}
41	    for key in buf[0]:
42	        vals = [m[key] for m in buf if key in m]
43	        agg[key] = sum(vals) / len(vals)
44	    composer._step_metrics = []
45	    return agg

48	class AdvantageWeightedComposer:
49	    """
50	    Normalizes each reward component's advantages per prompt-group before combining.
51	
52	    Motivation (DIET §3.2): raw reward variance σ²≈C(1-C) differs across components
53	    (e.g., binary accuracy has high variance; partial-credit format has low variance).
54	    Naive weighted sum lets high-variance components dominate the gradient signal
55	    regardless of assigned weight. Normalizing each component's rewards to
56	    zero-mean unit-std before summing ensures weights faithfully control contribution.
57	
58	    Per-group normalization: GRPO advantages are computed within each prompt-group
59	    (n_rollouts completions for one prompt). When `per_device_train_batch_size > 1`,
60	    the reward function receives multiple groups concatenated. Z-scoring across
61	    that concatenation conflates rewards across different prompts, distorting the
62	    relative ranking inside each group. We z-score per group instead.
63	    """
64	
65	    def __init__(self, components: list[tuple[Callable, float]]) -> None:
66	        self.components = components
67	        self.__name__ = "advantage_weighted_composer"
68	        # Per-step diagnostics, drained by a TrainerCallback (T2.1). Purely
69	        # observational — never read back into the composed reward.
70	        self._step_metrics: list[dict] = []
71	
72	    def __call__(self, prompts, completions, **kwargs) -> list[float]:
73	        import torch
74	
75	        n = len(completions)
76	        total = [0.0] * n
77	        groups = _group_indices(prompts)
78	
79	        call_metrics: dict[str, float] = {}
80	        for fn, weight in self.components:
81	            raw = fn(prompts, completions, **kwargs)
82	            r = torch.tensor(raw, dtype=torch.float32)
83	            normalized = torch.zeros_like(r)
84	            for idx in groups:
85	                if not idx:
86	                    continue
87	                slice_idx = torch.tensor(idx, dtype=torch.long)
88	                sub = r[slice_idx]
89	                std = sub.std()
90	                if std < 1e-6:
91	                    # Constant signal across the group carries no advantage
92	                    # information (every rollout gets the same value), so it
93	                    # contributes 0 to the composed reward regardless of its
94	                    # assigned weight. This is by design — there is no GRPO
95	                    # gradient to extract from a zero-variance signal — but
96	                    # it can surprise ablations where a saturated component
97	                    # (e.g. format_exact at 100% match) appears to have its
98	                    # weight ignored.
99	                    continue
100	                normalized[slice_idx] = (sub - sub.mean()) / std
101	            # weight * normalized is exactly the old `weight * v` per element —
102	            # the composed reward is unchanged; we only also record diagnostics.
103	            contribution = weight * normalized
104	            for i, v in enumerate(contribution.tolist()):
105	                total[i] += v
106	            name = type(fn).__name__
107	            call_metrics[f"reward/{name}/raw_mean"] = float(r.mean())
108	            call_metrics[f"reward/{name}/raw_std"] = float(r.std(unbiased=False))
109	            call_metrics[f"reward/{name}/contrib_l1"] = float(contribution.abs().mean())
110	
111	        self._step_metrics.append(call_metrics)
112	        return total
113	
114	    def pop_step_metrics(self) -> dict:
115	        return _drain_step_metrics(self)
116

118	class NaiveSumComposer:
119	    """Plain weighted sum — ablation baseline for E3.
120	    Contrast with AdvantageWeightedComposer to measure DIET advantage-weighting effect.
121	    """
122	
123	    def __init__(self, components: list[tuple[Callable, float]]) -> None:
124	        self.components = components
125	        self.__name__ = "naive_sum_composer"
126	        self._step_metrics: list[dict] = []
127	
128	    def __call__(self, prompts, completions, **kwargs) -> list[float]:
129	        n = len(completions)
130	        total = [0.0] * n
131	
132	        call_metrics: dict[str, float] = {}
133	        for fn, weight in self.components:
134	            raw = fn(prompts, completions, **kwargs)
135	            for i in range(n):
136	                total[i] += weight * raw[i]
137	            if n:
138	                mean = sum(raw) / n
139	                var = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in raw) / n
140	                name = type(fn).__name__
141	                call_metrics[f"reward/{name}/raw_mean"] = float(mean)
142	                call_metrics[f"reward/{name}/raw_std"] = float(var ** 0.5)
143	                call_metrics[f"reward/{name}/contrib_l1"] = float(sum(abs(weight * x) for x in raw) / n)
144	
145	        self._step_metrics.append(call_metrics)
146	        return total
147	
148	    def pop_step_metrics(self) -> dict:
149	        return _drain_step_metrics(self)
150	
151	
152	def build_composer(
153	    components: list[tuple[Callable, float]],
154	    method: str = "advantage_weighted",
155	) -> AdvantageWeightedComposer | NaiveSumComposer:
156	    if method == "advantage_weighted":
157	        return AdvantageWeightedComposer(components)
158	    if method == "naive_sum":
159	        return NaiveSumComposer(components)
160	    raise ValueError(f"Unknown compose_method: {method!r}. Choose advantage_weighted | naive_sum")

81	def warn_inert_scalars(rewards_cfg: dict, compose_method: str) -> list[str]:
82	    """Return warnings for reward knobs that do nothing as configured.

117	def validate_config(config: dict) -> None:
118	    """Validate config in-place-free: never mutates the input dict.
119	
120	    A previous version coerced int fields to floats via _set_nested, which
121	    leaked floats (e.g. max_steps: 500.0) into the frozen runs/<exp>/config.yaml.
122	    Range checks now operate on a local float copy only.
123	    """
124	    errors = []
125	
126	    for key, label in _REQUIRED_KEYS.items():
127	        if _get_nested(config, key) is None:
128	            errors.append(f"Missing required field: {label}")
129	
130	    # Agentic-only: every config runs against an OpenEnv environment.
131	    mode = (config.get("training") or {}).get("mode", "agentic")
132	    if mode != "agentic":
133	        errors.append(f"training.mode={mode!r}: only 'agentic' is supported")
134	    if _get_nested(config, "training.env") is None:
135	        errors.append("Missing required field: training.env (str) - OpenEnv environment id")
136	
137	    for key, (lo, hi) in _NUMERIC_COERCIONS.items():
138	        val = _get_nested(config, key)
139	        if val is None:
140	            continue
141	        try:
142	            fval = float(val)
143	        except (TypeError, ValueError):
144	            errors.append(f"Field {key}={val!r} is not numeric")
145	            continue
146	        if not (lo <= fval <= hi):
147	            errors.append(f"Field {key}={val} out of range [{lo}, {hi}]")
148	
149	    slug = _get_nested(config, "model.slug")
150	    if slug is not None:
151	        from training.registry import MODEL_REGISTRY
152	        if slug not in MODEL_REGISTRY:
153	            errors.append(
154	                f"model.slug={slug!r} not in registry. Available: {list(MODEL_REGISTRY)}"
155	            )
156	        else:
157	            # Cross-check lora_r against the registry's max for this model;
158	            # _NUMERIC_COERCIONS upper bound (256) is permissive across all models.
159	            lora_r = _get_nested(config, "model.lora_r")
160	            max_rank = MODEL_REGISTRY[slug].get("max_lora_rank")
161	            if lora_r is not None and max_rank is not None:
162	                try:
163	                    if int(lora_r) > int(max_rank):
164	                        errors.append(
165	                            f"model.lora_r={lora_r} exceeds registry max_lora_rank={max_rank} for slug={slug!r}"
166	                        )
167	                except (TypeError, ValueError):
168	                    pass
169	
170	    compose = _get_nested(config, "rewards.compose_method")
171	    if compose is not None and compose not in ("advantage_weighted", "naive_sum"):
172	        errors.append(
173	            f"rewards.compose_method={compose!r} must be 'advantage_weighted' or 'naive_sum'"
174	        )
175	
176	    rewards = config.get("rewards") or {}
177	    unknown_rewards = set(rewards.keys()) - _KNOWN_REWARD_KEYS
178	    if unknown_rewards:
179	        errors.append(
180	            f"Unknown rewards keys: {sorted(unknown_rewards)}. Known: {sorted(_KNOWN_REWARD_KEYS)}"
181	        )
182	
183	    for reward_name in _KNOWN_REWARD_SUBKEYS:        # excludes compose_method (a string)
184	        val = rewards.get(reward_name)
185	        if val is not None and not isinstance(val, dict):
186	            errors.append(
187	                f"rewards.{reward_name} must be a mapping (e.g. {{enabled: false}}), "
188	                f"got {type(val).__name__}: {val!r}"
189	            )
190	
191	    for reward_name, allowed in _KNOWN_REWARD_SUBKEYS.items():
192	        sub = rewards.get(reward_name)
193	        if not isinstance(sub, dict):
194	            continue
195	        unknown_sub = set(sub.keys()) - allowed
196	        if unknown_sub:
197	            errors.append(
198	                f"Unknown sub-keys under rewards.{reward_name}: {sorted(unknown_sub)}. "
199	                f"Allowed: {sorted(allowed)}"
200	            )
201	
202	    env_config = (config.get("training") or {}).get("env_config")
203	    if isinstance(env_config, dict):
204	        unknown_ec = set(env_config) - _KNOWN_ENV_CONFIG_KEYS
205	        if unknown_ec:
206	            errors.append(
207	                f"Unknown training.env_config keys: {sorted(unknown_ec)}. "
208	                f"Known: {sorted(_KNOWN_ENV_CONFIG_KEYS)}"
209	            )
210	
211	    eval_cfg = config.get("eval")
212	    if isinstance(eval_cfg, dict):
213	        unknown_eval = set(eval_cfg) - _KNOWN_EVAL_KEYS
214	        if unknown_eval:
215	            errors.append(
216	                f"Unknown eval keys: {sorted(unknown_eval)}. Known: {sorted(_KNOWN_EVAL_KEYS)}"
217	            )
218	        agentic = eval_cfg.get("agentic")
219	        if isinstance(agentic, dict):
220	            unknown_ag = set(agentic) - _KNOWN_EVAL_AGENTIC_KEYS
221	            if unknown_ag:
222	                errors.append(
223	                    f"Unknown eval.agentic keys: {sorted(unknown_ag)}. "
224	                    f"Known: {sorted(_KNOWN_EVAL_AGENTIC_KEYS)}"
225	                )
226	
227	    unknown_top = set(config.keys()) - _KNOWN_TOP_LEVEL_KEYS
228	    if unknown_top:
229	        errors.append(
230	            f"Unknown top-level keys: {sorted(unknown_top)}. Known: {sorted(_KNOWN_TOP_LEVEL_KEYS)}"
231	        )
232	
233	    if errors:
234	        msg = "Config validation failed:\n" + "\n".join(f" - {e}" for e in errors)
235	        raise ValueError(msg)

20	class _ComponentMetricsCallback(TrainerCallback):
21	    """Drain the composer's per-component reward metrics into the trainer log.
22	
23	    TRL only sees one composed reward function, so it logs a single
24	    rewards/<composer>/{mean,std}; the individual env/length/entropy
25	    contributions are invisible. transformers.Trainer.log() appends the log
26	    entry to state.log_history BEFORE calling on_log, so updating `logs` alone
27	    is too late — the persisted entry is already a copy. We update that
28	    just-appended entry in place (state.log_history[-1]) so the metrics land in
29	    train_log.json next to reward/kl/loss, and also update `logs` for any live
30	    logger (wandb/trackio). Purely observational: it never touches the composed
31	    reward or the advantage math.
32	    """
33	
34	    def __init__(self, composer) -> None:
35	        self.composer = composer
36	
37	    def on_log(self, args, state, control, logs=None, **kwargs):
38	        if not hasattr(self.composer, "pop_step_metrics"):
39	            return
40	        metrics = self.composer.pop_step_metrics()
41	        if not metrics:
42	            return
43	        # state.log_history[-1] is this step's entry (appended just before this
44	        # hook fires); update it in place so the metrics persist to train_log.
45	        if logs is not None:
46	            logs.update(metrics)
47	        if state is not None and getattr(state, "log_history", None):
48	            state.log_history[-1].update(metrics)

96	def apply_smoke_overrides(config: dict) -> dict:
97	    """Patch config for fast smoke testing: 3 steps, 2 rollouts, short seq.
98	
99	    Sets `_smoke=True` so downstream eval also caps to 10 samples per split.
100	    """
101	    config.setdefault("model", {})
102	    config.setdefault("training", {})
103	    # Pick a smoke context that clears the env's prompt but fits the L4. A 512 cap
104	    # rejected finqa's ~700-token tool-rich prompt outright; the full 4096 OOMs the
105	    # policy-grad backward under vLLM colocate. 2048 holds the prompt plus a few
106	    # turns and leaves room for the step. (Don't go below the config when it is
107	    # already smaller, e.g. a 1024-context model.)
108	    seq = min(int(config["model"].get("max_seq_length", 2048) or 2048), 2048)
109	    config["model"]["max_seq_length"] = seq
110	    # Under colocate the backward competes with vLLM's KV pool for the 24 GB, so
111	    # give training headroom in smoke (0.6 util OOMs a full agentic rollout here).
112	    # Set before --vllm's setdefault so this wins.
113	    config["model"]["gpu_memory_utilization"] = min(
114	        float(config["model"].get("gpu_memory_utilization", 0.45) or 0.45), 0.45
115	    )
116	    # Safety: the completion budget is max_seq - max_prompt_length, so keep the
117	    # prompt cap at half the context (a config with max_prompt_length == max_seq
118	    # would otherwise leave zero room to generate).
119	    config["training"]["max_prompt_length"] = min(
120	        int(config["training"].get("max_prompt_length", seq // 2) or seq // 2), seq // 2
121	    )
122	    config["training"]["max_steps"] = 3
123	    config["training"]["save_steps"] = 3
124	    config["training"]["n_rollouts"] = 2
125	    config["training"]["dataset_size_limit"] = 64
126	    # Cap eval generation: a multi-turn agentic eval runs many model.generate
127	    # calls per episode, and the default budget (max_seq - max_prompt) lets each
128	    # produce ~1k tokens, so a smoke eval can take 20+ minutes. 256 is plenty to
129	    # emit a tool call for a sanity check.
130	    config.setdefault("eval", {})
131	    config["eval"]["max_new_tokens"] = 256
132	    config["_smoke"] = True
133	    print(f"⚠  Smoke mode: max_steps=3, n_rollouts=2, max_seq_length={seq} (<=2048), "
134	          f"gpu_memory_utilization={config['model']['gpu_memory_utilization']}, "
135	          f"max_prompt_length={config['training']['max_prompt_length']}, dataset_size_limit=64, eval=10/split")
136	    return config

1	class ReasoningGymEnvAdapter:
2	    """TRL environment_factory adapter for the OpenEnv reasoning_gym env.
3	
4	    TRL's GRPOTrainer creates one instance per rollout slot, calls reset(**row)
5	    (whose return becomes the prompt), exposes every *other* public method as a
6	    tool the model may call, and reads the task reward off `self.reward`. The
7	    public surface is therefore deliberately exactly {reset, answer}: any extra
8	    public method would be registered as a tool and shown to the model.
9	
10	    The adapter wraps a *synchronous* OpenEnv client (EnvClient.sync()). The
11	    client and action class are injectable so the unit tests exercise the
12	    adapter logic without the OpenEnv install or a running server. reasoning_gym
13	    is single-step: one answer ends the episode.
14	    """
15	
16	    def __init__(self, base_url, env_config=None, client=None, action_cls=None):
17	        self._env_config = dict(env_config or {})
18	        self._client = client if client is not None else self._connect(base_url)
19	        self._action_cls = action_cls
20	        self.reward = 0.0
21	
22	    @staticmethod
23	    def _connect(base_url):
24	        # Lazy: the reasoning_gym client lives in the cloned OpenEnv repo's
25	        # envs/ package (not on PyPI), and EnvClient is async by default - the
26	        # .sync() wrapper is required because TRL rejects async tools.
27	        from reasoning_gym_env import ReasoningGymEnv
28	
29	        return ReasoningGymEnv(base_url).sync()
30	
31	    def _action(self, answer):
32	        if self._action_cls is None:
33	            from reasoning_gym_env import ReasoningGymAction
34	
35	            self._action_cls = ReasoningGymAction
36	        return self._action_cls(answer=answer)
37	
38	    def reset(self, *, seed=None, prompt=None, **_row):
39	        """Reset to a fresh reasoning_gym question; return the question text.
40	
41	        TRL appends the returned string to the prompt's last user message, then
42	        applies the tool-calling chat template. `prompt` and any other dataset
43	        columns arrive here as kwargs and are ignored - only `seed` selects the
44	        question (deterministic), with dataset name/config from env_config. size
45	        is pinned to 1: one question per episode for this single-step env.
46	        """
47	        reset_kwargs = {"size": 1}
48	        name = self._env_config.get("dataset_name") or self._env_config.get("dataset")
49	        if name is not None:
50	            reset_kwargs["dataset_name"] = name
51	        dataset_config = self._env_config.get("dataset_config")
52	        if dataset_config is not None:
53	            reset_kwargs["dataset_config"] = dataset_config
54	        if seed is not None:
55	            reset_kwargs["seed"] = seed
56	        result = self._client.reset(**reset_kwargs)
57	        self.reward = 0.0
58	        return result.observation.question
59	
60	    def answer(self, answer: str) -> str:
61	        """Submit your final answer to the current problem.
62	
63	        TRL renders this method into the tool spec the model sees, so the
64	        summary above and the Args description below are the tool's
65	        model-facing documentation. transformers' get_json_schema requires a
66	        Google-style Args entry for every parameter.
67	
68	        Args:
69	            answer: The final answer to submit for the current question.
70	        """
71	        result = self._client.step(self._action(answer))
72	        self.reward = float(result.observation.score)
73	        return f"Recorded answer: {answer}"

1	class EnvReward:
2	    """Task-success reward computed by the OpenEnv environment.
3	
4	    Under TRL's environment_factory path the trainer passes the live env
5	    instances to every reward function as kwargs['environments']. Each env has
6	    stored its episode reward on `env.reward` (set by the adapter's answer tool
7	    when the model submitted its answer). This component surfaces that
8	    per-completion reward to the composer so it is z-scored and weighted exactly
9	    like any code-computed reward.
10	    """
11	
12	    def __call__(self, prompts, completions, **kwargs):
13	        environments = kwargs.get("environments")
14	        if environments is None:
15	            raise ValueError(
16	                "EnvReward requires kwargs['environments'] from the agentic "
17	                "environment_factory path (TRL GRPOTrainer)."
18	            )
19	        if len(environments) != len(completions):
20	            raise ValueError(
21	                f"environments length {len(environments)} != completions {len(completions)}"
22	            )
23	        return [float(env.reward) for env in environments]

3	from domains.env_base import CORRECT_REWARD_THRESHOLD
4	from training.rewards.utils import model_token_count

6	
7	class CosineLengthReward:
8	    """Correctness-coupled cosine length reward (Wu/Yeo 2025, "Demystifying
9	    Long CoT"; Kimi-style length scaling).
10	
11	    For a completion of `n_tokens`, let progress = min(n_tokens / max_len, 1)
12	    and c = cos(progress * pi) - so c = +1 for an empty completion and c = -1
13	    at the length cap. The reward interpolates between a short-end and a
14	    long-end value, with the endpoints chosen by correctness:
15	
16	        correct: short -> r_correct_short, long -> r_correct_long   (short > long)
17	        wrong:   short -> r_wrong_short,   long -> r_wrong_long     (short < long)
18	
19	    Correct answers are rewarded more when shorter (concise reasoning); wrong
20	    answers are penalized less when longer (don't punish the model for thinking
21	    before failing). Wrong-and-short is therefore the most-penalized cell.
22	
23	    Under the default `advantage_weighted` composer every component is z-scored
24	    per prompt-group, which cancels any global positive scalar. A purely monotone
25	    signal (e.g. a plain length penalty) z-scores to pure rank order - "shorter
26	    always ranks higher" - so the model drives length to the format-envelope
27	    floor. This reward is non-linear in length *and* gated by correctness, so it
28	    survives z-scoring with real structure: a wrong 17-token completion lands in
29	    the worst cell instead of the best one.
30	
31	    Tradeoff: the length signal now carries correctness information, partially
32	    overlapping the `env_reward` component. That is acceptable under independent
33	    per-component z-scoring and is the intended Wu/Yeo coupling.
34	
35	    Agentic-only: correctness is read from the live OpenEnv instances TRL passes
36	    as kwargs['environments'] (env.reward >= CORRECT_REWARD_THRESHOLD; graded
37	    scorers hand partial credit to near-misses, so a bare > 0 gates wrong).
38	    There is no answer column.
39	    """
40	
41	    def __init__(
42	        self,
43	        tokenizer,
44	        max_len: int,
45	        r_correct_short: float = 1.0,
46	        r_correct_long: float = 0.5,
47	        r_wrong_short: float = -1.0,
48	        r_wrong_long: float = -0.5,
49	    ) -> None:
50	        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
51	        self.max_len = max(int(max_len), 1)
52	        self.r_correct_short = r_correct_short
53	        self.r_correct_long = r_correct_long
54	        self.r_wrong_short = r_wrong_short
55	        self.r_wrong_long = r_wrong_long
56	
57	    def _reward(self, n_tokens: int, correct: bool) -> float:
58	        progress = min(n_tokens / self.max_len, 1.0)
59	        c = math.cos(progress * math.pi)  # +1 at length 0, -1 at max_len
60	        if correct:
61	            lo, hi = self.r_correct_long, self.r_correct_short
62	        else:
63	            lo, hi = self.r_wrong_long, self.r_wrong_short
64	        return lo + 0.5 * (hi - lo) * (1.0 + c)
65	
66	    def __call__(self, prompts, completions, **kwargs) -> list[float]:
67	        # Agentic (environment_factory): TRL passes the live env instances as
68	        # kwargs['environments']; correctness is env.reward > 0 (no answer column).
69	        environments = kwargs.get("environments")
70	        if environments is None:
71	            raise ValueError(
72	                "CosineLengthReward requires kwargs['environments'] (agentic mode). "
73	                "TRL's environment_factory path supplies the live env instances."
74	            )
75	        correct_flags = [
76	            float(getattr(e, "reward", 0.0)) >= CORRECT_REWARD_THRESHOLD
77	            for e in environments
78	        ]
79	        # Prefer the exact model-generated token ids TRL/the rollout_func provide
80	        # over re-encoding decoded text, so the length signal counts model tokens
81	        # only. Falls back to re-encoding the decoded completion.
82	        provided_ids = kwargs.get("completion_ids")
83	        scores = []
84	        for i, completion in enumerate(completions):
85	            ids_i = provided_ids[i] if (provided_ids is not None and i < len(provided_ids)) else None
86	            n_tokens = self._n_tokens(completion, ids_i)
87	            scores.append(self._reward(n_tokens, correct_flags[i]))
88	        return scores
89	
90	    @staticmethod
91	    def _is_multiturn(completion) -> bool:
92	        # Multi-turn iff TRL interleaved a tool-result (game feedback) message.
93	        # In that case completion_ids over-counts (it includes tool tokens), so
94	        # fall back to the assistant-only re-encode.
95	        return isinstance(completion, list) and any(
96	            isinstance(m, dict) and m.get("role") == "tool" for m in completion
97	        )
98	
99	    def _n_tokens(self, completion, completion_ids_i) -> int:
100	        # Single-turn: prefer the exact model-generated ids TRL provides (no
101	        # re-encode) - keeps reasoning_gym numbers identical. Multi-turn: count
102	        # assistant tokens only, excluding injected feedback.
103	        if not self._is_multiturn(completion) and completion_ids_i is not None:
104	            return len(completion_ids_i)
105	        return model_token_count(completion, self.tokenizer)

2	    """TRL environment_factory adapter for the OpenEnv repl env (multi-turn).
3	
4	    TRL's GRPOTrainer creates one instance per rollout slot, calls reset(**row)
5	    (whose return becomes the prompt), exposes every *other* public method as a
6	    tool the model may call, and reads the task reward off `self.reward`. The
7	    public surface is exactly {reset, execute}: one tool, `execute(code)`, since
8	    repl is a Python REPL the model drives until it prints its final answer.
9	
10	    repl is a bare execution sandbox with no task source of its own, so unlike
11	    reasoning_gym the TASK is supplied by us: reset(**row) forwards `context`,
12	    `task_prompt`, and `expected_answer` (the ground truth) from the dataset row
13	    into the server, which sets them on its exact-match rubric. The reward is
14	    binary (1.0 if the model's FINAL(answer) matches expected_answer, else 0.0;
15	    a small negative on a no-answer timeout), populated as the episode ends.
16	
17	    Multi-turn: the model calls execute() repeatedly under stdout feedback until
18	    it prints FINAL(answer) (or the iteration cap), so the adapter keeps
19	    `self.done` like textarena and refreshes `self.reward` every step (non-final
20	    steps carry process reward, the final step carries the outcome).
21	
22	    The client is injectable so the unit tests exercise the adapter logic without
23	    the OpenEnv install or a running server.
24	    """
25	
26	    def __init__(self, base_url, env_config=None, client=None):
27	        self._env_config = dict(env_config or {})
28	        self._client = client if client is not None else self._connect(base_url)
29	        self.reward = 0.0
30	        self.done = False
31	
32	    @staticmethod
33	    def _connect(base_url):
34	        # Lazy: the repl client lives in the cloned OpenEnv repo's envs/ package
35	        # (not on PyPI). REPLEnv is an EnvClient; .sync() wraps it for TRL (which
36	        # rejects async tools), matching the textarena/reasoning_gym pattern.
37	        from repl_env import REPLEnv
38	
39	        return REPLEnv(base_url).sync()
40	
41	    def reset(self, *, seed=None, prompt=None, **_row):
42	        """Derive this seed's task, send it to the server, return the task text.
43	
44	        TRL appends the returned string to the prompt's last user message, then
45	        applies the tool-calling chat template. Only `seed` matters: the task is
46	        a pure function of the seed (make_task), so training and eval both call
47	        reset(seed=N) and get the identical task - no extra dataset columns, and
48	        the server-side exact-match rubric is armed with the seed's
49	        expected_answer. `prompt` and other columns arrive as kwargs and are
50	        ignored.
51	        """
52	        from domains.repl.tasks import make_task
53	
54	        context, task_prompt, expected_answer = make_task(seed if seed is not None else 0)
55	        self._client.reset(
56	            context=context, task_prompt=task_prompt, expected_answer=expected_answer,
57	            seed=seed,
58	        )
59	        self.reward = 0.0
60	        self.done = False
61	        return task_prompt
62	
63	    def execute(self, code: str) -> str:
64	        """Run Python in the REPL and read stdout. Finish by printing FINAL(answer).
65	
66	        State persists across calls (variables stay defined). To submit your
67	        final answer, print it as FINAL(<answer>) - e.g. print("FINAL(42)") -
68	        which ends the episode.
69	
70	        TRL renders this method into the tool spec the model sees, so this
71	        summary and the Args description below are the tool's model-facing
72	        documentation. transformers' get_json_schema requires a Google-style Args
73	        entry for every parameter.
74	
75	        Args:
76	            code: A snippet of Python to execute in the persistent REPL.
77	        """
78	        if self.done:
79	            # Done-guard: once a final answer is recorded, further code cannot
80	            # corrupt the terminal reward.
81	            return "The task is already answered; no further code is accepted."
82	        # step(REPLAction) is the canonical path (matches textarena/finqa); the
83	        # client's execute() convenience wraps the same call.
84	        from repl_env import REPLAction
85	
86	        result = self._client.step(REPLAction(code=code))
87	        self.reward = float(getattr(result, "reward", 0.0) or 0.0)
88	        self.done = bool(getattr(result, "done", False))
89	        return self._feedback_text(result)
90	
91	    @staticmethod
92	    def _feedback_text(result) -> str:
93	        # Return the REPL's stdout for the model's next turn, plus the error if
94	        # the snippet raised. The observation carries a CodeBlockResult (stdout /
95	        # stderr / exception); fall back gracefully if shapes differ.
96	        obs = getattr(result, "observation", None)
97	        block = getattr(obs, "result", None)
98	        if block is None:
99	            return str(getattr(result, "observation", "") or "")
100	        out = str(getattr(block, "stdout", "") or "")
101	        exc = getattr(block, "exception", None)
102	        err = str(getattr(block, "stderr", "") or "")
103	        parts = [p for p in (out, exc or err) if p]
104	        return "\n".join(parts) if parts else "(no output)"

7	## 1. Liger fused GRPO loss - lift the 4096 completion-token training ceiling
8	
9	Training completions are capped at 4096 tokens because the policy update
10	materialises four full `[T, 151936]` bf16 tensors per completion (logits, the
11	`log_softmax` output, and a gradient for each), about 4.6 GiB at T=4096 on top
12	of a ~14.4 GiB resident base. 6144 OOMs. The cap is what produces the
13	truncation confound that corrupted e9-e21 and still leaves 7-8% of e24/e25
14	episodes cut off mid-reasoning.
15	
16	`use_liger_kernel` is a TRL `BaseConfig` field (default `False`). When set,
17	`GRPOTrainer` builds `LigerFusedLinearGRPOLoss` and routes the loss through
18	`compute_liger_loss` instead of `_get_per_token_logps_and_entropies`. The fused
19	path folds the LM head matmul into the loss and chunks over the sequence, so
20	the full `[T, vocab]` tensor is never allocated. transformers claims ~60% memory
21	reduction. If it holds here, 16k training becomes reachable on the L4 with no
22	new hardware and no precision change.
23	
24	Not verified yet:
25	
26	- `liger_kernel` is not installed on the box (`pip install liger-kernel`); TRL
27	  raises `ImportError` if the flag is set without it.
28	- Whether the released liger-kernel supports Qwen3.
29	- Whether `LigerFusedLinearGRPOLoss` composes with `environment_factory` and the
30	  multi-turn tool masking the agentic path depends on.
31	
32	Steps:

34	1. Install liger-kernel on the box.
35	2. Add `use_liger_kernel` passthrough in `_grpo_config` (`training/grpo_runner.py`).

39	   equivalent and not just cheaper.
40	5. Memcheck at 16k. If it fits, the cap question is closed.

5	# Reduce CUDA allocator fragmentation so vLLM colocate + training coexist on a
6	# 24 GB GPU. Must be set before torch initializes the caching allocator.
7	os.environ.setdefault("PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF", "expandable_segments:True")
