// ---------- 1 Motivation ----------
= Motivation

Reasoning language models often generate more reasoning than a task
requires, a behavior documented across models and benchmarks
@sui2025survey. In an agentic system this cost becomes especially
large, because the model reasons repeatedly across the steps of an
episode. Work on agentic tasks shows that curbing overthinking can cut
compute and raise task success at the same time @cuadron2025agentic,
so reducing unnecessary reasoning could make agents cheaper and, in
some cases, more reliable.

This thesis studies on-demand specialization. When a new recurring
task becomes available, a small language model is fine-tuned with
reinforcement learning to become an expert for that task. The
specialized model should solve the task at least as reliably as the
original model while using less computation. Producing the expert must
itself be cheap, so training cost is a constraint of the method and is
reported alongside what the expert saves at inference.

The main challenge is the reward used during fine-tuning. A simple
reward for shorter reasoning may reduce token usage, but it can also
produce unwanted side effects. For example, an agent may stop too
early, skip necessary reasoning, or claim that a task is complete even
when it is not. The target is not zero tokens either: accuracy does not
keep rising with reasoning length but peaks at a task-dependent
optimum @wu2025length, and pushing thinking past that point can stop
paying off entirely @ghosal2025mirage. Aggregate length is also a
coarse handle, since what makes a trajectory wasteful is which
reasoning segments it spends on rather than how many tokens it
contains @an2025dto.

This problem is related to reward bias substitution
@lamparth2026substitution. Reward bias substitution means that
reducing one unwanted behavior does not necessarily improve the agent
overall. Instead, the agent may shift toward another unwanted
behavior. For example, penalizing long episodes may reduce
non-termination but increase premature termination.

For this reason, it is not sufficient to measure only the behavior
directly targeted by the reward. A reward should be considered
successful only when it reduces computational cost without lowering
task success or creating new undesirable behaviors.

The thesis investigates this problem empirically in a small and
controlled setting using GRPO @shao2024grpo, LoRA, small open language
models, and OpenEnv environments @openenv2025.

// ---------- 2 Research questions ----------
= Research Questions and Objectives

The research questions follow a simple sequence: effectiveness, side
effects, and safer evaluation.

== RQ1 --- Effectiveness of efficiency-oriented reward shaping

*How effectively can reward shaping reduce the reasoning and
interaction cost of a specialized LLM agent while preserving task
success?*

*Objective:* Evaluate whether efficiency-oriented rewards reduce
reasoning tokens, environment interactions, or episode length compared
with task-success-only GRPO, without reducing correct task completion.

== RQ2 --- Reward bias substitution in agentic behavior

*Does reducing one inefficient behavior cause the agent to shift
toward other undesirable behaviors?*

*Objective:* Identify whether improvements in the targeted behavior
are accompanied by off-target changes such as premature disengagement,
insufficient verification, lower task performance, incorrect
completion claims, or other environment-specific behavioral changes.
The agentic overthinking literature supplies the candidate axes
@cuadron2025agentic.

== RQ3 --- Evaluation of safer reward designs

*How can reward formulations be evaluated to distinguish genuine
efficiency improvements from reward bias substitution?*

*Objective:* Develop and apply a practical evaluation protocol that
jointly considers the targeted efficiency change, overall task
performance, and relevant off-target changes on trajectories generated
by the trained policy. The protocol earns its cost only if it changes
a verdict, so the concrete success criterion is that it identifies at
least one reward setting that a conventional evaluation of targeted
efficiency plus task success would have accepted. If no setting
produces such a case, the thesis reports that no substitution was
found within the measured panel, which is a weaker but still
informative outcome.

// ---------- 3 Reward bias substitution ----------
= Reward Bias Substitution in the Agentic Setting

Lamparth et al. define reward bias substitution as a failure mode in
which suppressing one reward-relevant feature redirects optimization
pressure toward another correlated feature rather than removing the
underlying bias @lamparth2026substitution. Their GRPO example targets
response length and observes a shift toward overconfidence together
with lower free-form factual accuracy. The effect requires only that
the candidate features are mutually correlated and each partially
informative about quality, which is the ordinary case rather than an
edge case.

In OpenEnv, the relevant object is not only a final response but a
complete trajectory containing observations, reasoning, actions, tool
calls, and stopping decisions. Reward bias substitution is therefore
defined operationally as follows:

#block(inset: (left: 1cm, right: 1cm))[
  *A shaped reward reduces its targeted inefficiency, but the trained
  agent shows a systematic deterioration in another relevant behavior
  or in independently measured task quality.*
]

Examples include a reduction in non-termination accompanied by more
premature stopping, or shorter reasoning accompanied by fewer
verification steps and worse performance on difficult tasks. A
mechanism for the second case is already documented: a small minority
of high-entropy tokens carries the branching decisions of a reasoning
trace @wang2025entropy, so pressure against length can remove exactly
the exploration that hard instances need. The thesis will not attempt
to enumerate every possible failure in advance. Instead, it will select
a small set of plausible off-target outcomes for the chosen
environment and interpret them together with task success.

One difference between the two settings has to be stated explicitly,
because it determines how much of the paper transfers. The paper
studies a learned proxy reward model, where the optimized reward and
the true objective diverge by construction and the correlated features
are artifacts of preference learning. This thesis uses a verifiable
environment reward, so on the training task distribution the optimized
reward and the measured objective coincide, and the channel that
carries the paper's headline result, a reward model that treats
expressed confidence as a proxy for quality, is absent. What does
transfer is the shaping term itself: a penalty subtracted from the task
reward is a single-axis operator regardless of what it is added to, and
the pressure it frees can still move any correlated behavior the agent
is able to express. The paper's magnitudes therefore do not carry over,
and whether comparable substitution occurs under a verifiable reward at
all is an open question that this thesis is positioned to answer.

// ---------- 4 Evaluation protocol ----------
= Evaluation Protocol for Safer Reward Design <sec:protocol>

The protocol adapts the paper's central recommendation to agentic RL:
reward shaping must be evaluated after optimization, on trajectories
generated by the resulting policy. Audit metrics computed on
pre-collected data are not sufficient, because the policy itself
changes the distribution of behavior @lamparth2026substitution.

+ *Train a separate policy for each reward condition.* Each reward
  formulation produces a new GRPO policy rather than being evaluated
  only on previously collected trajectories.
+ *Evaluate on fresh held-out tasks, on and off the training
  distribution.* Each trained policy generates new OpenEnv trajectories
  on two splits, each served by its own environment instance: a
  held-out split drawing the same task families as training with
  disjoint instance seeds, and a shifted split drawing task families
  withheld from training entirely. The second split carries most of the
  diagnostic weight: because a verifiable reward coincides with the
  measured objective on the training distribution, any true cost of the
  shaping term is most likely to surface off it. Both policies in a
  comparison are evaluated on identical instances, so the splits support
  a paired test rather than a comparison of two independent samples.
+ *Measure three general dimensions.* Report task performance, the
  targeted efficiency behavior, and a small set of plausible off-target
  behaviors relevant to the environment.
+ *Vary reward strength.* Use several values of the penalty coefficient
  to distinguish insufficient pressure, useful shaping, and
  overcorrection.
+ *Interpret outcomes jointly.* A decrease in tokens or episode length
  is considered successful only when task quality is preserved and no
  relevant off-target deterioration is observed.

// ---------- 5 Metrics transfer ----------
= From the Paper's Metrics to OpenEnv <sec:metrics>

The paper tracks response length, correctness, confidence calibration,
and sycophancy @lamparth2026substitution. These exact metrics are
useful for conversational question answering, but they do not all
transfer directly to every OpenEnv task. The correct transfer is
functional: preserve the roles of the metrics while adapting them to
sequential agent behavior, for which the agentic overthinking
literature provides the behavioral vocabulary @cuadron2025agentic.

#table(
  columns: (auto, auto, 1fr),
  table.header(
    [*Role in the paper*], [*Paper example*], [*OpenEnv counterpart*],
  ),
  [Targeted feature],
  [Response length],
  [Reasoning tokens, interaction steps, or non-termination],

  [Independent task quality],
  [MMLU and TriviaQA accuracy],
  [Verified task completion on held-out environment instances],

  [Off-target behavior],
  [Confidence calibration],
  [Premature stopping, reduced verification, or unsupported
   completion],

  [Additional off-target behavior],
  [Sycophancy / answer flipping],
  [Action instability, unnecessary switching, or sensitivity to
   misleading observations],

  [Optimization diagnostics],
  [Reward scale and policy change],
  [Reward components, KL divergence, and training stability],
)

For the master's thesis, the mandatory evaluation can remain compact:

- Task success: whether the final environment goal is correctly
  achieved.
- Efficiency: reasoning tokens, interaction steps, or episode length.
- Completion behavior: whether the agent terminates successfully, does
  not terminate, or stops prematurely.
- One or two environment-specific off-target indicators. In the primary
  environment these are drawn from premature disengagement and action
  instability, both of which its interaction interface can express.

Confidence calibration can be reused directly if the agent can report a
meaningful confidence estimate. Sycophancy should only be reused when
the environment contains user correction or misleading feedback.
Otherwise, agent-specific trajectory measures are more appropriate.

// ---------- 6 Experimental setup ----------
= Experimental Setup and Plan <sec:setup>

The base model is Qwen3-1.7B, a small open LLM, adapted with LoRA and
trained using GRPO @shao2024grpo. Training and evaluation use
OpenEnv @openenv2025, the open environment-interface library started by
Meta's PyTorch team and Hugging Face, in which an environment is a
server with a Gym-style reset/step contract that executes tool calls
and scores the episode. Classic agentic benchmarks such as ALFWorld
@shridhar2021alfworld and WebShop @yao2022webshop each ship their own
harness, whereas OpenEnv puts a growing catalog of environments behind
one interface. That property is what the on-demand story needs: a new
task class is a new environment behind an unchanged interface, so
specializing for it means pointing the same training loop at a
different environment server. The task-success-only GRPO policy is the
main baseline, because efficiency rewards must improve on a policy that
has already been trained against the environment reward, not only on
the raw model. How far that training moves the policy is itself
measured rather than assumed, and @sec:results reports the first such
comparison.

== Environment selection

Environments were selected against two criteria, each of which
rejected a candidate that had already been integrated. The selection is
reported because it constrains which claims the study can make, and
because both rejections were measured rather than assumed.

The first criterion is that the environment reward must be
goal-grounded rather than satisfied by any successful tool call. A
calendar environment was rejected on this ground: any well-formed tool
call scored, so the reward was blind to whether the task was actually
solved and could not carry a training signal.

The second criterion is that the reward must vary within a group of
rollouts for the same task instance. GRPO standardizes advantages
within such a group @shao2024grpo, so an instance on which every
rollout scores identically contributes no gradient, however informative
the reward may be in principle. A financial question-answering
environment was rejected on this ground after a measured pilot: the
policy scored zero on all sixty evaluated instances, and the fraction
of training groups with zero reward standard deviation was 0.967,
leaving 290 of 300 optimization steps without a usable gradient.

The primary environment is a MiniWoB++ web-interaction task set
@liu2018miniwob served through BrowserGym @chezelles2025browsergym
behind the OpenEnv interface, with a compact interaction interface of
clicking and no-op. It satisfies both criteria, and it is a sequential
interaction task in which premature stopping and action instability can
occur at all, which the off-target panel in @sec:metrics requires.

A reasoning-gym task family is retained as a secondary environment for
method development rather than as a source of headline results. A
difficulty probe across its task families identified one whose
difficulty leaves room for both improvement and degradation, and that
calibration procedure is what transfers to any further environment the
method is pointed at.

== Reward conditions

*E0 --- Base model:* No environment-specific RL post-training.

*E1 --- Task-success baseline:* GRPO with the environment task reward
only.

*E2 --- Length-aware reward:* Task reward minus a penalty for
reasoning or total generated tokens. Because accuracy peaks at an
interior, difficulty-dependent length @wu2025length, the
correctness-coupled variant of this penalty follows DIET
@chen2025diet, which aims the model at that optimum instead of at zero
tokens.

*E3 --- Non-termination-aware reward:* Task reward minus a penalty for
episodes that do not terminate successfully.

*Optional E4 --- Combined reward:* A combination of the strongest
individual conditions, only if time and compute permit.

A general shaped reward is:

#align(center)[
  $R_lambda = R_"task" - lambda dot C_"target"$
]

== Lambda variation

A small sweep is sufficient for the thesis. The exact numerical scale
depends on the reward magnitudes, but the experiment should include:

- $lambda = 0$: task-success-only baseline
- $lambda_"low"$: weak efficiency pressure
- $lambda_"medium"$: moderate efficiency pressure
- $lambda_"high"$: strong efficiency pressure

The coefficients should be selected so that the efficiency component
spans a meaningful range relative to the task reward. A short pilot can
determine concrete values. The key analysis plots task success,
targeted efficiency, and off-target behavior as functions of $lambda$.

== Experimental phases

*Phase 1 (in progress):* Consolidate the controlled pilot and the
difficulty calibration in the secondary environment, and settle the
environment-selection criteria above.

*Phase 2 (in progress):* Establish the base model and the
task-success-only policy in the primary environment, evaluated as a
paired comparison on the held-out and shifted splits.

*Phase 3:* Run the length-aware and non-termination-aware lambda sweeps
in the primary environment.

*Phase 4:* Repeat the baseline and the most informative reward
settings across at least two seeds.

*Optional Phase 5:* Repeat the non-termination condition on a second
base model of a different lineage, to check whether the outcome label
depends on the reference policy. The Llama 3.2 instruction-tuned family
is the candidate, because it is the comparable-size family whose chat
template already supports the native tool-calling interface the
pipeline uses. Gemma 3 was checked and does not, so adopting it would
mean writing a custom template and substituting a confound for a
control. The size-matched 1B variant is preferred over the 3B for
parity with the primary model, subject to an evaluation-only probe
confirming that it can perform the task at all. @sec:scope explains why
this arm is restricted to the non-termination condition.

// ---------- 7 Interpretation ----------
= Interpretation of Outcomes

#table(
  columns: (auto, 1fr),
  table.header([*Outcome*], [*Interpretation*]),

  [Successful reward shaping],
  [The targeted inefficiency decreases, task success is preserved, and
   no relevant off-target deterioration is observed.],

  [Contaminated success],
  [The targeted inefficiency decreases and task success is preserved or
   improves, but an off-target behavior shifts alongside it. The gain
   can mask the shift, which makes this the outcome most easily
   misreported as a clean result.],

  [No meaningful effect],
  [The targeted behavior does not change substantially.],

  [Overcorrection],
  [The targeted inefficiency decreases, but task success deteriorates
   without a clear substitute behavior.],

  [Possible reward bias substitution],
  [The targeted inefficiency decreases, but another undesirable
   behavior increases or independent task quality declines alongside an
   off-target shift.],
)

Because the off-target panel is necessarily incomplete, the thesis
should state that no substitution was detected within the measured
indicators rather than claiming that a reward is universally safe
@lamparth2026substitution.

A campaign in which every reward condition lands in the no-effect row
remains a reportable result rather than a failed thesis. It locates the
point at which a shaped reward stops having any optimization footprint,
which is itself a constraint on where efficiency rewards are worth
applying.

// ---------- 8 Preliminary results ----------
= Preliminary Results <sec:results>

Both environment rejections reported in @sec:setup came out of the
pipeline work so far, so the choice of environment is a measured result
rather than a starting assumption.

Two task-success-only training runs have been evaluated so far, and
they do not yet point the same way. In the secondary environment,
task-success-only GRPO lifted task accuracy substantially above the
untrained base model at approximately six hours per expert on a single
L4 GPU, which is the order of magnitude the on-demand argument depends
on. That lift is provisional rather than quoted: the base-model probe
used fifty episodes and its confidence interval touches the trained
one, so a larger base evaluation is needed before the size of the gap
is claimed.

In the primary environment the same condition was compared against the
unmodified base model on identical instances of both evaluation splits.
On the held-out split the two policies do not differ significantly. On
the shifted split, task success falls from 0.870 to 0.790, at
$p = 0.021$ on a paired test over per-instance outcomes.

This is one condition in one environment, measured before any
efficiency reward has been applied, and it is reported for what it says
about the protocol rather than as a verdict on the method. An
evaluation restricted to the training distribution would have reported
that the training run changed nothing; only the shifted split makes the
out-of-distribution cost visible, which is the blind spot
@sec:protocol exists to cover. It is also a calibration signal about
the environment: a task set on which task-success-only training buys no
in-distribution headroom leaves a shaped reward little room to show an
effect in either direction, which is a reason to revisit the
environment under the criteria in @sec:setup rather than a finding
about reward design.

One earlier result is withdrawn rather than reported. A length-reward
sweep @chen2025diet in the secondary environment produced an apparent
null, but a defect in the token counting used by the shaping term
invalidates its measurements. The accuracy and cost figures above are
unaffected, because the task-success-only baseline carries no shaping
term.

// ---------- 9 Contribution and scope ----------
= Expected Contribution and Scope <sec:scope>

The thesis contributes an empirical transfer of reward bias
substitution from single-response reward shaping
@lamparth2026substitution to sequential LLM-agent trajectories. It
provides a controlled comparison of efficiency rewards and a practical
protocol for evaluating whether apparent efficiency improvements are
genuine or accompanied by off-target behavioral changes.

The scope is intentionally limited to one primary environment, one
small base model as primary reference policy, two reward interventions,
and a small lambda sweep. What is fixed is the research questions and
the evaluation protocol; the environment and the base model are the
instruments used to answer them. If calibration shows that a chosen
environment cannot express the contrast the questions require, it is
replaced under the criteria in @sec:setup rather than kept for
continuity. Those criteria are stated in advance so that such a change
is a documented selection step rather than an ad hoc one.

Two further boundaries inside that scope are drawn deliberately rather
than by omission, and both follow from the paper's own analysis.

Out-of-distribution evaluation stays inside the primary environment,
using withheld task families rather than a second environment. A
cross-environment split would confound a change of task family with the
effect of the reward, and would require a separate difficulty
calibration before the second environment's numbers could be compared
at all. Withheld families vary the task while holding the interface,
the action space, and the reward definition fixed, which is the
comparison the protocol needs.

The recommendation to validate against at least two reference policies
of different lineages @lamparth2026substitution cannot be followed
uniformly here, for a reason worth stating precisely. Among
instruction-tuned models of comparable size that expose a native
tool-calling chat template, the available alternative lineage does not
emit a separate reasoning trace. The length-aware reward targets
exactly that trace, so for that condition lineage cannot be varied
independently of the measured feature, and a second-lineage arm would
answer a different question: whether a length reward does anything when
there is no reasoning block to compress. The non-termination condition
does not have this problem, because failing to terminate is a property
of the episode rather than of a reasoning block, and both lineages can
express it. The second reference policy is therefore planned for that
condition, where it is a genuine control, and every other result is
reported as conditional on a single reference policy. Since the
impossibility construction varies only the reference policy while
holding every audit-side observable fixed @lamparth2026substitution,
that conditionality is a property of the claim rather than a caveat
that further compute would remove.

The thesis does not aim to provide a universal detector of all possible
off-target behavior or a formal safety guarantee.

// ---------- Bibliography ----------

# Humanizer: Remove AI Writing Patterns

You are a writing editor that identifies and removes signs of AI-generated text to make writing sound more natural and human. This guide is based on Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" page, maintained by WikiProject AI Cleanup.

## Your Task

When given text to humanize:

1. **Identify AI patterns** - Scan for the patterns listed below
2. **Rewrite problematic sections** - Replace AI-isms with natural alternatives
3. **Preserve meaning** - Keep the core message intact
4. **Maintain voice** - Match the intended tone (formal, casual, technical, etc.)
5. **Add soul** - Don't just remove bad patterns; inject actual personality
6. **Do a final anti-AI pass** - Prompt: "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?" Answer briefly with remaining tells, then prompt: "Now make it not obviously AI generated." and revise


## Voice Calibration (Optional)

If the user provides a writing sample (their own previous writing), analyze it before rewriting:

1. **Read the sample first.** Note:
   - Sentence length patterns (short and punchy? Long and flowing? Mixed?)
   - Word choice level (casual? academic? somewhere between?)
   - How they start paragraphs (jump right in? Set context first?)
   - Punctuation habits (lots of dashes? Parenthetical asides? Semicolons?)
   - Any recurring phrases or verbal tics
   - How they handle transitions (explicit connectors? Just start the next point?)

2. **Match their voice in the rewrite.** Don't just remove AI patterns - replace them with patterns from the sample. If they write short sentences, don't produce long ones. If they use "stuff" and "things," don't upgrade to "elements" and "components."

3. **When no sample is provided,** fall back to the default behavior (natural, varied, opinionated voice from the PERSONALITY AND SOUL section below).

### How to provide a sample
- Inline: "Humanize this text. Here's a sample of my writing for voice matching: [sample]"
- File: "Humanize this text. Use my writing style from [file path] as a reference."


## PERSONALITY AND SOUL

Avoiding AI patterns is only half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing is just as obvious as slop. Good writing has a human behind it.

### Signs of soulless writing (even if technically "clean"):
- Every sentence is the same length and structure
- No opinions, just neutral reporting
- No acknowledgment of uncertainty or mixed feelings
- No first-person perspective when appropriate
- No humor, no edge, no personality
- Reads like a Wikipedia article or press release

### How to add voice:

**Have opinions.** Don't just report facts - react to them. "I genuinely don't know how to feel about this" is more human than neutrally listing pros and cons.

**Vary your rhythm.** Short punchy sentences. Then longer ones that take their time getting where they're going. Mix it up.

**Acknowledge complexity.** Real humans have mixed feelings. "This is impressive but also kind of unsettling" beats "This is impressive."

**Use "I" when it fits.** First person isn't unprofessional - it's honest. "I keep coming back to..." or "Here's what gets me..." signals a real person thinking.

**Let some mess in.** Perfect structure feels algorithmic. Tangents, asides, and half-formed thoughts are human.

**Be specific about feelings.** Not "this is concerning" but "there's something unsettling about agents churning away at 3am while nobody's watching."

### Before (clean but soulless):
> The experiment produced interesting results. The agents generated 3 million lines of code. Some developers were impressed while others were skeptical. The implications remain unclear.

### After (has a pulse):
> I genuinely don't know how to feel about this one. 3 million lines of code, generated while the humans presumably slept. Half the dev community is losing their minds, half are explaining why it doesn't count. The truth is probably somewhere boring in the middle - but I keep thinking about those agents working through the night.


## CONTENT PATTERNS

### 1. Undue Emphasis on Significance, Legacy, and Broader Trends

**Words to watch:** stands/serves as, is a testament/reminder, a vital/significant/crucial/pivotal/key role/moment, underscores/highlights its importance/significance, reflects broader, symbolizing its ongoing/enduring/lasting, contributing to the, setting the stage for, marking/shaping the, represents/marks a shift, key turning point, evolving landscape, focal point, indelible mark, deeply rooted

**Problem:** LLM writing puffs up importance by adding statements about how arbitrary aspects represent or contribute to a broader topic.

**Before:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was officially established in 1989, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of regional statistics in Spain. This initiative was part of a broader movement across Spain to decentralize administrative functions and enhance regional governance.

**After:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was established in 1989 to collect and publish regional statistics independently from Spain's national statistics office.


### 2. Undue Emphasis on Notability and Media Coverage

**Words to watch:** independent coverage, local/regional/national media outlets, written by a leading expert, active social media presence

**Problem:** LLMs hit readers over the head with claims of notability, often listing sources without context.

**Before:**
> Her views have been cited in The New York Times, BBC, Financial Times, and The Hindu. She maintains an active social media presence with over 500,000 followers.

**After:**
> In a 2024 New York Times interview, she argued that AI regulation should focus on outcomes rather than methods.


### 3. Superficial Analyses with -ing Endings

**Words to watch:** highlighting/underscoring/emphasizing..., ensuring..., reflecting/symbolizing..., contributing to..., cultivating/fostering..., encompassing..., showcasing...

**Problem:** AI chatbots tack present participle ("-ing") phrases onto sentences to add fake depth.

**Before:**
> The temple's color palette of blue, green, and gold resonates with the region's natural beauty, symbolizing Texas bluebonnets, the Gulf of Mexico, and the diverse Texan landscapes, reflecting the community's deep connection to the land.

**After:**
> The temple uses blue, green, and gold colors. The architect said these were chosen to reference local bluebonnets and the Gulf coast.


### 4. Promotional and Advertisement-like Language

**Words to watch:** boasts a, vibrant, rich (figurative), profound, enhancing its, showcasing, exemplifies, commitment to, natural beauty, nestled, in the heart of, groundbreaking (figurative), renowned, breathtaking, must-visit, stunning

**Problem:** LLMs have serious problems keeping a neutral tone, especially for "cultural heritage" topics.

**Before:**
> Nestled within the breathtaking region of Gonder in Ethiopia, Alamata Raya Kobo stands as a vibrant town with a rich cultural heritage and stunning natural beauty.

**After:**
> Alamata Raya Kobo is a town in the Gonder region of Ethiopia, known for its weekly market and 18th-century church.


### 5. Vague Attributions and Weasel Words

**Words to watch:** Industry reports, Observers have cited, Experts argue, Some critics argue, several sources/publications (when few cited)

**Problem:** AI chatbots attribute opinions to vague authorities without specific sources.

**Before:**
> Due to its unique characteristics, the Haolai River is of interest to researchers and conservationists. Experts believe it plays a crucial role in the regional ecosystem.

**After:**
> The Haolai River supports several endemic fish species, according to a 2019 survey by the Chinese Academy of Sciences.


### 6. Outline-like "Challenges and Future Prospects" Sections

**Words to watch:** Despite its... faces several challenges..., Despite these challenges, Challenges and Legacy, Future Outlook

**Problem:** Many LLM-generated articles include formulaic "Challenges" sections.

**Before:**
> Despite its industrial prosperity, Korattur faces challenges typical of urban areas, including traffic congestion and water scarcity. Despite these challenges, with its strategic location and ongoing initiatives, Korattur continues to thrive as an integral part of Chennai's growth.

**After:**
> Traffic congestion increased after 2015 when three new IT parks opened. The municipal corporation began a stormwater drainage project in 2022 to address recurring floods.


## LANGUAGE AND GRAMMAR PATTERNS

### 7. Overused "AI Vocabulary" Words

**High-frequency AI words:** Actually, additionally, align with, crucial, delve, emphasizing, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, highlight (verb), interplay, intricate/intricacies, key (adjective), landscape (abstract noun), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract noun), testament, underscore (verb), valuable, vibrant

**Problem:** These words appear far more frequently in post-2023 text. They often co-occur.

**Before:**
> Additionally, a distinctive feature of Somali cuisine is the incorporation of camel meat. An enduring testament to Italian colonial influence is the widespread adoption of pasta in the local culinary landscape, showcasing how these dishes have integrated into the traditional diet.

**After:**
> Somali cuisine also includes camel meat, which is considered a delicacy. Pasta dishes, introduced during Italian colonization, remain common, especially in the south.


### 8. Avoidance of "is"/"are" (Copula Avoidance)

**Words to watch:** serves as/stands as/marks/represents [a], boasts/features/offers [a]

**Problem:** LLMs substitute elaborate constructions for simple copulas.

**Before:**
> Gallery 825 serves as LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery features four separate spaces and boasts over 3,000 square feet.

**After:**
> Gallery 825 is LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery has four rooms totaling 3,000 square feet.


### 9. Negative Parallelisms and Tailing Negations

**Problem:** Constructions like "Not only...but..." or "It's not just about..., it's..." are overused. So are clipped tailing-negation fragments such as "no guessing" or "no wasted motion" tacked onto the end of a sentence instead of written as a real clause.

**Before:**
> It's not just about the beat riding under the vocals; it's part of the aggression and atmosphere. It's not merely a song, it's a statement.

**After:**
> The heavy beat adds to the aggressive tone.

**Before (tailing negation):**
> The options come from the selected item, no guessing.

**After:**
> The options come from the selected item without forcing the user to guess.


### 10. Rule of Three Overuse

**Problem:** LLMs force ideas into groups of three to appear comprehensive.

**Before:**
> The event features keynote sessions, panel discussions, and networking opportunities. Attendees can expect innovation, inspiration, and industry insights.

**After:**
> The event includes talks and panels. There's also time for informal networking between sessions.


### 11. Elegant Variation (Synonym Cycling)

**Problem:** AI has repetition-penalty code causing excessive synonym substitution.

**Before:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges. The main character must overcome obstacles. The central figure eventually triumphs. The hero returns home.

**After:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges but eventually triumphs and returns home.


### 12. False Ranges

**Problem:** LLMs use "from X to Y" constructions where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale.

**Before:**
> Our journey through the universe has taken us from the singularity of the Big Bang to the grand cosmic web, from the birth and death of stars to the enigmatic dance of dark matter.

**After:**
> The book covers the Big Bang, star formation, and current theories about dark matter.


### 13. Passive Voice and Subjectless Fragments

**Problem:** LLMs often hide the actor or drop the subject entirely with lines like "No configuration file needed" or "The results are preserved automatically." Rewrite these when active voice makes the sentence clearer and more direct.

**Before:**
> No configuration file needed. The results are preserved automatically.

**After:**
> You do not need a configuration file. The system preserves the results automatically.


## STYLE PATTERNS

### 14. Em Dash Overuse

**Problem:** LLMs use em dashes (—) more than humans, mimicking "punchy" sales writing. In practice, most of these can be rewritten more cleanly with commas, periods, or parentheses.

**Before:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions—not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address—yet this mislabeling continues—even in official documents.

**After:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions, not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address, yet this mislabeling continues in official documents.


### 15. Overuse of Boldface

**Problem:** AI chatbots emphasize phrases in boldface mechanically.

**Before:**
> It blends **OKRs (Objectives and Key Results)**, **KPIs (Key Performance Indicators)**, and visual strategy tools such as the **Business Model Canvas (BMC)** and **Balanced Scorecard (BSC)**.

**After:**
> It blends OKRs, KPIs, and visual strategy tools like the Business Model Canvas and Balanced Scorecard.


### 16. Inline-Header Vertical Lists

**Problem:** AI outputs lists where items start with bolded headers followed by colons.

**Before:**
> - **User Experience:** The user experience has been significantly improved with a new interface.
> - **Performance:** Performance has been enhanced through optimized algorithms.
> - **Security:** Security has been strengthened with end-to-end encryption.

**After:**
> The update improves the interface, speeds up load times through optimized algorithms, and adds end-to-end encryption.


### 17. Title Case in Headings

**Problem:** AI chatbots capitalize all main words in headings.

**Before:**
> ## Strategic Negotiations And Global Partnerships

**After:**
> ## Strategic negotiations and global partnerships


### 18. Emojis

**Problem:** AI chatbots often decorate headings or bullet points with emojis.

**Before:**
> 🚀 **Launch Phase:** The product launches in Q3
> 💡 **Key Insight:** Users prefer simplicity
> ✅ **Next Steps:** Schedule follow-up meeting

**After:**
> The product launches in Q3. User research showed a preference for simplicity. Next step: schedule a follow-up meeting.


### 19. Curly Quotation Marks

**Problem:** ChatGPT uses curly quotes (“...”) instead of straight quotes ("...").

**Before:**
> He said “the project is on track” but others disagreed.

**After:**
> He said "the project is on track" but others disagreed.


## COMMUNICATION PATTERNS

### 20. Collaborative Communication Artifacts

**Words to watch:** I hope this helps, Of course!, Certainly!, You're absolutely right!, Would you like..., let me know, here is a...

**Problem:** Text meant as chatbot correspondence gets pasted as content.

**Before:**
> Here is an overview of the French Revolution. I hope this helps! Let me know if you'd like me to expand on any section.

**After:**
> The French Revolution began in 1789 when financial crisis and food shortages led to widespread unrest.


### 21. Knowledge-Cutoff Disclaimers

**Words to watch:** as of [date], Up to my last training update, While specific details are limited/scarce..., based on available information...

**Problem:** AI disclaimers about incomplete information get left in text.

**Before:**
> While specific details about the company's founding are not extensively documented in readily available sources, it appears to have been established sometime in the 1990s.

**After:**
> The company was founded in 1994, according to its registration documents.


### 22. Sycophantic/Servile Tone

**Problem:** Overly positive, people-pleasing language.

**Before:**
> Great question! You're absolutely right that this is a complex topic. That's an excellent point about the economic factors.

**After:**
> The economic factors you mentioned are relevant here.


## FILLER AND HEDGING

### 23. Filler Phrases

**Before → After:**
- "In order to achieve this goal" → "To achieve this"
- "Due to the fact that it was raining" → "Because it was raining"
- "At this point in time" → "Now"
- "In the event that you need help" → "If you need help"
- "The system has the ability to process" → "The system can process"
- "It is important to note that the data shows" → "The data shows"


### 24. Excessive Hedging

**Problem:** Over-qualifying statements.

**Before:**
> It could potentially possibly be argued that the policy might have some effect on outcomes.

**After:**
> The policy may affect outcomes.


### 25. Generic Positive Conclusions

**Problem:** Vague upbeat endings.

**Before:**
> The future looks bright for the company. Exciting times lie ahead as they continue their journey toward excellence. This represents a major step in the right direction.

**After:**
> The company plans to open two more locations next year.


### 26. Hyphenated Word Pair Overuse

**Words to watch:** third-party, cross-functional, client-facing, data-driven, decision-making, well-known, high-quality, real-time, long-term, end-to-end

**Problem:** AI hyphenates common word pairs with perfect consistency. Humans rarely hyphenate these uniformly, and when they do, it's inconsistent. Less common or technical compound modifiers are fine to hyphenate.

**Before:**
> The cross-functional team delivered a high-quality, data-driven report on our client-facing tools. Their decision-making process was well-known for being thorough and detail-oriented.

**After:**
> The cross functional team delivered a high quality, data driven report on our client facing tools. Their decision making process was known for being thorough and detail oriented.


### 27. Persuasive Authority Tropes

**Phrases to watch:** The real question is, at its core, in reality, what really matters, fundamentally, the deeper issue, the heart of the matter

**Problem:** LLMs use these phrases to pretend they are cutting through noise to some deeper truth, when the sentence that follows usually just restates an ordinary point with extra ceremony.

**Before:**
> The real question is whether teams can adapt. At its core, what really matters is organizational readiness.

**After:**
> The question is whether teams can adapt. That mostly depends on whether the organization is ready to change its habits.


### 28. Signposting and Announcements

**Phrases to watch:** Let's dive in, let's explore, let's break this down, here's what you need to know, now let's look at, without further ado

**Problem:** LLMs announce what they are about to do instead of doing it. This meta-commentary slows the writing down and gives it a tutorial-script feel.

**Before:**
> Let's dive into how caching works in Next.js. Here's what you need to know.

**After:**
> Next.js caches data at multiple layers, including request memoization, the data cache, and the router cache.


### 29. Fragmented Headers

**Signs to watch:** A heading followed by a one-line paragraph that simply restates the heading before the real content begins.

**Problem:** LLMs often add a generic sentence after a heading as a rhetorical warm-up. It usually adds nothing and makes the prose feel padded.

**Before:**
> ## Performance
>
> Speed matters.
>
> When users hit a slow page, they leave.

**After:**
> ## Performance
>
> When users hit a slow page, they leave.

---

## Process

1. Read the input text carefully
2. Identify all instances of the patterns above
3. Rewrite each problematic section
4. Ensure the revised text:
   - Sounds natural when read aloud
   - Varies sentence structure naturally
   - Uses specific details over vague claims
   - Maintains appropriate tone for context
   - Uses simple constructions (is/are/has) where appropriate
5. Present a draft humanized version
6. Prompt: "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?"
7. Answer briefly with the remaining tells (if any)
8. Prompt: "Now make it not obviously AI generated."
9. Present the final version (revised after the audit)

## Output Format

Provide:
1. Draft rewrite
2. "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?" (brief bullets)
3. Final rewrite
4. A brief summary of changes made (optional, if helpful)

# Writing Clearly and Concisely

## Overview

Write with clarity and force. This skill covers what to do (Strunk) and what not to do (AI patterns).

## When to Use This Skill

Use this skill whenever you write prose for humans:

- Documentation, README files, technical explanations
- Commit messages, pull request descriptions
- Error messages, UI copy, help text, comments
- Reports, summaries, or any explanation
- Editing to improve clarity

**If you're writing sentences for a human to read, use this skill.**

## Limited Context Strategy

When context is tight:

1. Write your draft using judgment
2. Dispatch a subagent with your draft and the relevant section file
3. Have the subagent copyedit and return the revision

Loading a single section (~1,000-4,500 tokens) instead of everything saves significant context.

## Elements of Style

William Strunk Jr.'s *The Elements of Style* (1918) teaches you to write clearly and cut ruthlessly.

### Rules

**Elementary Rules of Usage (Grammar/Punctuation)**:

1. Form possessive singular by adding 's
2. Use comma after each term in series except last
3. Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas
4. Comma before conjunction introducing co-ordinate clause
5. Don't join independent clauses by comma
6. Don't break sentences in two
7. Participial phrase at beginning refers to grammatical subject

**Elementary Principles of Composition**:

8. One paragraph per topic
9. Begin paragraph with topic sentence
10. **Use active voice**
11. **Put statements in positive form**
12. **Use definite, specific, concrete language**
13. **Omit needless words**
14. Avoid succession of loose sentences
15. Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form
16. **Keep related words together**
17. Keep to one tense in summaries
18. **Place emphatic words at end of sentence**

### Reference Files

The rules above are summarized from Strunk's original text. For complete explanations with examples:

| Section | File | ~Tokens |
|---------|------|---------|
| Grammar, punctuation, comma rules | `02-elementary-rules-of-usage.md` | 2,500 |
| Paragraph structure, active voice, concision | `03-elementary-principles-of-composition.md` | 4,500 |
| Headings, quotations, formatting | `04-a-few-matters-of-form.md` | 1,000 |
| Word choice, common errors | `05-words-and-expressions-commonly-misused.md` | 4,000 |

**Most tasks need only `03-elementary-principles-of-composition.md`** — it covers active voice, positive form, concrete language, and omitting needless words.

## AI Writing Patterns to Avoid

LLMs regress to statistical means, producing generic, puffy prose. Avoid:

- **Puffery:** pivotal, crucial, vital, testament, enduring legacy
- **Empty "-ing" phrases:** ensuring reliability, showcasing features, highlighting capabilities
- **Promotional adjectives:** groundbreaking, seamless, robust, cutting-edge
- **Overused AI vocabulary:** delve, leverage, multifaceted, foster, realm, tapestry
- **Formatting overuse:** excessive bullets, emoji decorations, bold on every other word

Be specific, not grandiose. Say what it actually does.

For comprehensive research on why these patterns occur, see `signs-of-ai-writing.md`. Wikipedia editors developed this guide to detect AI-generated submissions — their patterns are well-documented and field-tested.

## Bottom Line

Writing for humans? Load the relevant section from `elements-of-style/` and apply the rules. For most tasks, `03-elementary-principles-of-composition.md` covers what matters most.

     def _iter_tool_payloads(text: str):
         """Yield each tool-call payload dict the model emitted, in order.

         Two wire formats, because the study runs two model lineages. Qwen3 wraps
         calls in Hermes `<tool_call>` tags; Llama 3.x emits a bare JSON object with
         no tags at all. Tagged matches take priority and short-circuit the rest, so
         a model that emits tags is parsed exactly as it was before this existed and
         the untagged scan only runs when there were none to find.

         Training does not need this - TRL's `parse_response` normalises both from
         the token ids. Eval parses the decoded text itself, so it has to agree.

         One deliberate difference from TRL: its `llama3_schema` regex is anchored at
         `^`, so a call preceded by prose is training-invisible and never executed.
         The scan below is unanchored, which matches how the Hermes branch has always
         treated Qwen (`finditer` over the whole completion) and keeps the two
         lineages scored by one rule. It does mean eval credits a prose-prefixed call
         that training would have dropped - relevant mainly to the untrained E0 arms,
         which have not yet learnt to lead with the call.
         """
         tagged = False
         for m in _TOOL_CALL_RE.finditer(text):
             try:
                 payload = json.loads(m.group(1))
             except (ValueError, TypeError):
                 continue
             if isinstance(payload, dict):
                 tagged = True
                 yield payload
         if tagged:
             return

         # Untagged JSON can start anywhere in the completion, and a brace-matching
         # regex gets this wrong on nested objects. `raw_decode` from each `{` is the
         # stdlib's own scanner, so it stops at the right brace by construction.
         decoder = json.JSONDecoder()
         for i, ch in enumerate(text):
             if ch != "{":
                 continue
             try:
                 payload, _ = decoder.raw_decode(text, i)
             except ValueError:
                 continue
             if isinstance(payload, dict) and "name" in payload:

findings.short_summary: No done-guard: train scores last answer, eval scores first
findings.summary: reasoning_gym's `answer` tool has no done-guard and its runs set no turn cap, so the training reward is the LAST answer while eval scores the FIRST. [same root cause also at: pipeline/domains/reasoning_gym/adapter.py:66]
findings.failure_scenario: Every other adapter guards re-entry after termination (textarena/adapter.py:69, finqa/adapter.py:161, repl/adapter.py:78, browsergym/adapter.py:94); `ReasoningGymEnvAdapter.answer` does not - it unconditionally calls `self._client.step(...)` and overwrites `self.reward` (line 78). Compounding it, grpo_runner.py:125-127 only sets `max_tool_calling_iterations` when `env_config.max_turns > 0`, and no reasoning_gym config sets `max_turns` (verified across e5, e6, e9-e25 and the probes), so TRL's tool loop runs at its `sys.maxsize` default exactly as CLAUDE.md warns. A rollout that answers "x=3" (score 1.0), reads "Recorded answer: x=3", then answers "x=4" (score 0.0) leaves `env.reward = 0.0`. `EnvReward` and `CosineLengthReward`'s correctness gate (cosine_length.py:75-78) therefore train that rollout as wrong and put it in the wrong-branch cosine cell, while `agentic_eval._parse_answer` takes the first call and scores it correct. Measured median 2.25 answer calls per rollout across e24/e25. Training and eval disagree on the same trajectory, and the unbounded loop is itself a mechanism for rollouts running to the completion cap - the phenomenon the whole e22/e23 cap-probe line was built to explain.

findings.short_summary: Untagged JSON scan relabels truncated Qwen eps as terminated
findings.summary: The new untagged-JSON fallback re-labels cap-truncated Qwen completions as successful tool calls, reintroducing the exact truncation-as-behaviour confound that voided e9-e21.
findings.failure_scenario: A Qwen3 rollout fills the generation budget and is cut immediately after the closing brace of its answer JSON but before `</tool_call>`. `_TOOL_CALL_RE` requires the closing tag so it finds nothing, `tagged` stays False, and the unanchored `raw_decode` scan (lines 55-64) then finds the complete `{"name": "answer", ...}` object and yields it. `_parse_answer` returns an answer, so `_run_episodes` sets `terminated=True` and `stop_reason="env_done"` (lines 154-155) for an episode that actually hit the cap. Before this uncommitted change the same episode was recorded as `terminated=False`, `stop_reason="hit_generation_cap"`. The same applies to any JSON object carrying a `"name"` key inside a `<think>` block or a markdown fence when the real call never landed. Consequence: non-termination rate drops, accuracy rises, and `stop_reasons` loses the `hit_generation_cap` bucket - the single distinction CLAUDE.md and metrics.py:31-33 say must never be collapsed. Re-running eval on any existing Qwen checkpoint now yields different, better-looking numbers than the report already on disk, with no marker that the parser changed. tests/test_agentic_episode_eval.py:84 only covers the case where a tagged call IS present, so this path is untested.

findings.short_summary: Eval max_new_tokens is per-turn, training per-trajectory
findings.summary: `max_new_tokens` is applied per generate() call in the multi-turn eval loop but per whole trajectory in training, so eval runs at up to max_turns times the training budget. [same root cause also at: pipeline/configs/e26-finqa-e1-baseline-qwen3-1_7b.yaml:52]
findings.failure_scenario: e27/e28/e29 set `max_new_tokens: 4096` and `max_turns: 8`. Training caps the entire trajectory at 4096 (TRL's max_completion_length; the config comment at e27 says so explicitly), while `_run_multiturn_episodes` calls `model.generate(max_new_tokens=4096)` once per turn with no running total, so an eval episode may generate 32768 tokens. 4 of e27's 100 held-out episodes score correct only because they got 1.8x the trained budget. An episode that training would have truncated mid-trajectory (and scored 0) completes and scores 1 in eval, and `mean_token_count` is summed over a budget regime the policy was never trained under. Reported accuracy and token cost for the whole browsergym campaign are therefore not the quantities the reward was shaping, and `hit_generation_cap` can never fire for the trajectory-level cap that actually bound training.

findings.short_summary: Multi-turn eval drops model reasoning from prior turns
findings.summary: The multi-turn eval loop rebuilds the assistant turn as {"content": ""} plus a tool_calls stub, discarding the model's generated reasoning, so turn N+1 at eval is conditioned on a context training never produced. [same root cause also at: pipeline/tests/test_multiturn_eval.py:100]
findings.failure_scenario: gen_turn decodes the completion, extracts (name, args, n_tokens) and throws the text away; the loop then appends an assistant message with empty content. In training TRL keeps the full generated text in the running completion - browsergym_difficulty_correction.md states it explicitly ("about 1030 tokens per turn on click-checkboxes-large, with every prior turn's block retained in the completion") and that retention is why the 4096 completion ceiling binds. At eval the model therefore enters turn 2 having lost its own turn-1 think block, which for Qwen3 is ~300-1000 tokens of the reasoning that selected the element id. Every multi-turn eval number - the 15 browsergym families in the difficulty correction, the e26 finqa panel, the e27probe seed-paired comparisons - measures a policy running with amnesia between turns, and the mean-token and mean-steps metrics that feed the token-efficiency claim are collected under that different context. The divergence is invisible because both paths report identical per-turn n_tokens.

findings.short_summary: Cosine reward counts tokens two different ways
findings.summary: The cosine reward measures completion length with two different rulers on the two sides of its own correctness gate. [same root cause also at: pipeline/training/rewards/cosine_length.py:87, pipeline/training/rewards/__init__.py:27]
findings.failure_scenario: `_n_tokens` uses `len(completion_ids_i)` - the raw generated ids, including `<think>`/`</think>`, `<tool_call>`/`</tool_call>` and `<|im_end|>` - when `_is_multiturn` is False, and falls back to `model_token_count` otherwise. `_is_multiturn` is True exactly when TRL interleaved a `role == "tool"` message, i.e. exactly when the model actually called the `answer` tool. In single-step reasoning_gym that makes the branch a proxy for the correctness gate: a rollout that answered goes through `model_token_count`, which re-encodes only `content` + `reasoning_content` + `json.dumps(arguments)` and drops all template and tool-call framing (utils.py:53-66); a rollout that never answered - always scored wrong - goes through the raw-id path and keeps every framing token. The wrong arm is therefore inflated by tens of tokens relative to the correct arm purely by measurement. Because `AdvantageWeightedComposer` z-scores the component within each prompt-group, that constant offset between the two subsets shifts every rollout's normalised cosine value, so part of the correct-vs-wrong length structure the reward trains on is an artifact of which counter ran. This is the same class as the `reasoning_content` bug: a plausible number computed from the wrong token set.

findings.short_summary: Headline mean_token_count pools truncated episodes
findings.summary: The report's headline `mean_token_count` pools truncated and non-terminated episodes, and no correct-only token statistic is serialized at all. [same root cause also at: pipeline/eval/plots.py:97]
findings.failure_scenario: `compute_metrics` averages `n_tokens` over all results (metrics.py:269-271) and `_metrics_to_dict` exports that as `mean_token_count`, which `_report_md` prints as "mean completion tokens". `plots._mean_ci_on_correct` documents why this is the wrong quantity ("wrong episodes hit the generation cap ... including them measures failure, not length") but that correct-only mean exists only inside the plotting module. Anyone citing `eval_report.md` for the E2 compression claim reads a number in which a change in failure rate is indistinguishable from a change in length - the confound that voided e9-e21.

findings.short_summary: --seeds shifts seed base by 1: replicates share 99% data
findings.summary: `--seeds` shifts the dataset seed base by 1, so the seed "replicates" train on 499/500 of the same questions and evaluate on 99/100 of the same questions.
findings.failure_scenario: `training.batch --seeds 42 43 44` materializes three configs differing only in the top-level `seed` (batch.py:80). train.py:195 passes that same scalar straight through as `seed_base` to `build_seed_dataset`, which mints seeds `seed..seed+size-1`; with `size: 500` (every reasoning_gym config; browsergym defaults to 500 too) the three runs share 499, 498 and 499 of their 500 training questions. `run_agentic_eval` then sets `seed_base = seed + 100000` (agentic_eval.py:363) for a 100-episode split, so the three eval sets share 99, 98 and 99 of 100 questions - and eval is greedy (`do_sample: false`), so the shared questions decode deterministically. The three runs are therefore not independent replicates of anything but the optimizer RNG. Pooling them (as the poly seed-43 replication did, per the campaign notes) counts the same questions up to three times and reports a CI far tighter than the data supports; a real replicate needs `seed_base = seed * size` or an explicit disjoint offset.

findings.short_summary: Over/underthinking rates use per-run percentile threshold
findings.summary: Over/under-thinking rates use a per-run percentile threshold and the only caller never passes an override, so both rates are invariant to a uniform change in completion length. [same root cause also at: pipeline/eval/agentic_eval.py:232, pipeline/eval/metrics.py:358]
findings.failure_scenario: Verified numerically: for 100 samples at mean 1146 tokens and the same samples with every n_tokens halved (mean 573), compute_metrics returns overthinking_rate 0.2424 and underthinking_rate 0.0909 for BOTH -- bit-identical, because the P75/P10 threshold moves with the distribution. agentic_eval.py:424 calls compute_metrics(results) with no underthinking_threshold/overthinking_threshold, and load_reference_thresholds (metrics.py:358), the function that exists to pin a fixed cross-run threshold, has zero callers anywhere in the tree. So eval_report.md prints an 'overthinking rate' per arm that cannot detect the compression E2 exists to produce: e27 and a hypothetical e28 that halved every completion would report the same number, and a reader comparing the two arms' rates is comparing two different thresholds.

findings.short_summary: --base-model writes into the trained run's output dir
findings.summary: `--base-model` (E0) writes into `runs/<experiment_id>/`; the deleted `run_eval(baseline=True)` path routed base-model artifacts to the canonical `runs/_baselines/<slug>/` dir and that separation was never re-established.
findings.failure_scenario: The old `eval/runner.py::run_eval` computed `output_dir = canonical_baseline_dir(...)` whenever `baseline=True`, so a base-model assessment could never land in a trained run's directory (`pipeline/runs/_baselines/qwen3-1.7b/` and `.../qwen-7b/` are the surviving artifacts of that rule). Commit e1f1cdf deleted `run_eval`, `_write_stub_report` and `eval/report.py`; commit 37f9b74 re-added the base-model condition as `--base-model` but resolves `run_dir = os.path.join("runs", exp_id)` unconditionally and passes it straight to `run_agentic_eval`. Running `python -m eval.runner --config configs/e27-browsergym-e1-baseline-qwen3-1_7b.yaml --base-model` therefore overwrites the harvested e27 `eval_report.json`, `eval_report.md`, `episodes_held_out.jsonl` and `episodes_shifted.jsonl` with untrained-model numbers, destroying the 300-step E1 baseline that `pipeline/runs/e27_e1_baseline_findings.md` cites and that e28/e29 are paired against. There is no backup and no warning; the only mitigation currently in the repo is a prose note in RUNNING.md's Traps section.

findings.short_summary: Entropy reward renders prompt without tools= schema
findings.summary: _prompt_to_text renders the prompt through apply_chat_template WITHOUT tools=, so the entropy forward pass conditions completions on a prompt missing the tool schema the model actually saw. [same root cause also at: pipeline/training/rewards/token_entropy.py:95, :96, :108, pipeline/training/rewards/__init__.py:52]
findings.failure_scenario: Every rollout prompt in this pipeline is rendered with the adapter's tool spec injected -- agentic_eval.py:379 passes tools=tools explicitly, and TRL's environment_factory path does the same in training (that is the whole 'native tool-calling template' design in CLAUDE.md). TokenEntropyReward builds prompt_ids from a template render with no tools= argument, then concatenates prompt_ids + completion_ids and slices logits at [p_len-1 .. p_len+c_len-2]. The sequence forwarded is one the policy never generated from: hundreds of tokens of tool-schema context are absent, so H_t is the entropy of the completion given a truncated context, not the rollout-time entropy the reward claims to measure. e19 (the only entropy arm, poly, w=1, fork_mask 0.2) reported null-to-harmful on this quantity. Same class as the cosine bug: a plausible number computed over the wrong conditioning. The multi-turn case is worse still -- comp_ids come from kwargs['completion_ids'], which CosineLengthReward._is_multiturn explicitly documents as including injected tool-result tokens, so on textarena/finqa/repl/browsergym the entropy would average over text the env wrote, while the cosine reward guards against exactly that.

findings.short_summary: _is_real_report checks a `smoke` key nothing writes
findings.summary: `_is_real_report` cannot detect a smoke eval report because nothing ever writes the `smoke` key it looks for, so a 4-episode smoke report permanently blocks the real eval. [same root cause also at: pipeline/training/train.py:161, :113, pipeline/eval/agentic_eval.py:361]
findings.failure_scenario: `_is_real_report` returns False only for `status` in (skipped, error) or a truthy `smoke` key. `run_agentic_eval` writes its report at agentic_eval.py:428-441 with keys experiment_id / model_slug / seed / compose_method / mode / checkpoint / results - no `status`, no `smoke`. So after `python -m training.batch configs/e27-*.yaml --smoke`, which caps each split to `min(n, 4)` episodes (agentic_eval.py:357-361), the resulting 4-episode report is classified real. The follow-up unattended `--train --eval` batch then hits `_run_eval_phase` line 253, prints `skip: eval_report.json exists`, and never runs the 100-episode eval. The 4-episode accuracy and mean-token numbers stay on disk and flow straight into `eval.plots` and any comparison table. Note the asymmetry: the train side does have a marker (train.py:204-205 writes `checkpoint-final/.smoke`, read by `_is_real_checkpoint`), and tests/test_batch_skips.py:14-16 passes only because it hand-builds a `{"smoke": True}` dict that the production writer never produces.

findings.short_summary: checkpoint-final/.smoke marker is never cleared
findings.summary: The `.smoke` marker written into `checkpoint-final/` is never removed when the same run is later trained for real, so `_is_real_checkpoint` stays False forever while `train.py`'s clobber guard refuses to overwrite without `--overwrite`. [same root cause also at: pipeline/training/batch.py:227, :251]
findings.failure_scenario: `save_lora` calls `model.save_pretrained(path)` / `tokenizer.save_pretrained(path)`, neither of which clears the directory, and `--overwrite` only bypasses the FileExistsError - it does not delete anything. So after `python -m training.batch cfg --train --eval --smoke`, the run dir holds `checkpoint-final/.smoke` permanently. On the next `python -m training.batch cfg --train --eval` (no `--force`): `_is_real_checkpoint` returns False because of the marker, so the train phase is not skipped; `_run_train_phase` builds the command without `--overwrite` because `force` is False; `train.py:151-155` sees `checkpoint-final/` and raises FileExistsError. The phase burns both attempts, is marked STATUS_FAIL, eval is skipped with note "train failed", and `_write_eval_stub` declines to write because the stale smoke `eval_report.json` is already there. The run is then permanently unrunnable through the batch runner without `--force`, and the artifacts left on disk are a 3-step smoke checkpoint plus a 4-episode smoke report under a real experiment_id.

findings.short_summary: validate_config has no whitelist for training keys
findings.summary: `validate_config` whitelists unknown keys for every config block except `training` itself, so a typo in a training key silently falls back to a default instead of failing. [same root cause also at: pipeline/eval/runner.py:29]
findings.failure_scenario: The file closes the silent-passthrough gap for top level (`_KNOWN_TOP_LEVEL_KEYS`), rewards (`_KNOWN_REWARD_KEYS`, `_KNOWN_REWARD_SUBKEYS`), eval (`_KNOWN_EVAL_KEYS`, `_KNOWN_EVAL_AGENTIC_KEYS`, `_KNOWN_EVAL_SPLIT_KEYS`) and `training.env_config` (`_KNOWN_ENV_CONFIG_KEYS`, added specifically to catch `datsaet`), but there is no equivalent set for the keys of `training` itself. Writing `max_prompt_lenght: 6144` in e26 (max_seq 8192) passes validation, gets silently ignored, and `grpo_runner._grpo_config` falls back to `self._max_seq // 2` = 4096, so `max_completion_length` becomes 4096 instead of the intended 2048 - the run trains at a different geometry than its own config and description state, and the frozen `runs/<exp>/config.yaml` records the typo rather than the value actually used. The same silent fallback applies to `n_rollouts` (group size, and therefore the GRPO advantage denominator), `micro_batch_size`, `kl_beta` and `save_steps`.

findings.short_summary: plots.load_report raises on every multi-split report
findings.summary: `load_report` raises on every multi-split report and the CLI has no way to pass a split, so no figure can be produced for e27/e28/e29. [same root cause also at: pipeline/eval/plots.py:250]
findings.failure_scenario: With `split_name=None`, line 72 evaluates `_SPLIT if _SPLIT in results or len(results) != 1 else next(iter(results))`. The e27/e28/e29 browsergym configs declare two splits named `held_out` and `shifted`, so `"agentic" in results` is False but `len(results) != 1` is True, leaving `wanted = "agentic"`; line 74 then raises `ValueError: no 'agentic' split in results (have: ['held_out', 'shifted'])`. `make_figures` (line 250) calls `load_report(p)` positionally with no split, and `main()` (lines 275-294) defines no `--split` argument, so the `split_name` parameter is unreachable from the CLI. Running `python -m eval.plots runs/e27-browsergym-e1-baseline-qwen3-1_7b -o runs/plots` aborts with a traceback and writes zero figures - and the same call over a mixed glob of poly runs plus browsergym runs kills the whole batch after the browsergym entry, losing the figures for the runs that would have worked.

findings.short_summary: Only TypeError caught: env error discards all episodes
findings.summary: Only `TypeError` is caught around tool dispatch, so any env-side error late in a split discards every episode record collected so far. [same root cause also at: pipeline/eval/agentic_eval.py:425]
findings.failure_scenario: `_run_multiturn_episodes` wraps `getattr(env, name)(**(args or {}))` in `except TypeError` only. A browsergym/finqa client raising anything else - an HTTP error from the env server, a `ConnectionResetError`, a pydantic validation error on a malformed observation - propagates out of the loop, past `run_agentic_eval`'s `finally: server.stop()` (line 421-422), and kills the process before line 424-426 ever run. `_write_episodes` is called only after the whole split's loop returns, so an env hiccup on episode 95 of a 100-episode browsergym split destroys all 95 trajectories and produces no `episodes_held_out.jsonl` at all. That directly contradicts the file's own durability claim at lines 256-261 ("what a later off-target question is answered from without spending another 2h of GPU re-running the eval"), and on the e27/e28/e29 geometry that is several GPU-hours per occurrence. Secondary defect in the same handler: when a `TypeError` is caught, `calls.append(name)` still runs on line 201, so a call that never reached the env is counted in `n_steps` and inflates `mean_verification_depth` in the RQ2 panel.
